div.head: First Scene.
div.stage: —The exterior of the Foundling Hospital. A dark night. The wind heard moaning. “The Lady,” plainly dressed, is discovered waiting at the door by which the nurses of the Foundling enter and leave the institution. The Lady listens at the door, then takes a turn on the stage, and returns to the door. At the same moment two or three nurses pass out. The Lady, after eyeing them carefully, one by one, under the lamp which is over the door, lets them go, without speaking to them. A pause after the last nurse has gone out. Sally Goldstraw appears at the door. The Lady recognises and stops her. The dialogue begins.

sp.speaker: The Lady,
sp.p: Stop!

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: What do you want, ma'am?

sp.speaker: The Lady.
sp.p: A word with you in private.

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Are you mistaking me for somebody else? I have never seen you before.

sp.speaker: The Lady.
sp.p: I saw you this morning. You were pointed out to me by a friend who was willing to assist me so far. You are known here as Sally Goldstraw. And you first entered this institution, on this very day, twelve years since. It was impossible for me to speak to you this morning, for it was impossible for me to see you in private. I must speak to you now.

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: You seem to know all about me, ma'am. Might I make so bold as to ask, who you are?

sp.speaker: The Lady.
sp.p: Come and look at me under the lamp.

sp.speaker: Sally
sp.p: I don't know you. I never saw you before to-night.

sp.speaker: The Lady.
sp.p: Do I look like a happy woman?

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: No, ma'am. You look as if you had something on your mind.

sp.speaker: The Lady.
sp.p: I have something on my mind. I am one of the many miserable mothers who have never known what a mother's happiness is. If my child is still living, he is in the Foundling Hospital—he has grown to be a boy, and I have never seen him!

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: I am heartily sorry for you, ma'am. But what can I do?

sp.speaker: The Lady.
sp.p: You can carry your memory back through twelve years. You can recal the day when you first entered that house.

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Twelve years is a long time, ma'am.

sp.speaker: The Lady.
sp.p: Is it long to you? Think how long it has been to me! Through all those years I have paid the penalty of disgracing my family. Through all those years I have lived in foreign lands—lived on the one condition that I should not be seen again in England. Only a week since I found myself independent of that condition—placed in the possession of a fortune—free to come back to my own country. Sally Goldstraw! I have come back with one hope. It lies in your power to make a happy woman of me.

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: How can I do that, ma'am?

sp.speaker: The Lady.
sp.p: Here are two guineas in this paper. Take my poor little present, and I will tell you.

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: You may know my face, ma'am; but you don't know me. There is not a person in all the Foundling who hasn't a good word for Sally. Could I be so well thought of if I was to be bought?

sp.speaker: The Lady.
sp.p: I do not mean to buy you. I only mean to reward you very slightly.

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: If helping you is right, ma'am, I desire no reward for doing it. What do you want?

sp.speaker: The Lady.
sp.p: I want you to look back through the past time. The day when you first entered the Foundling must be a marked day in your memory.

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: It is a marked day.

sp.speaker: The Lady.
sp.p: You may have forgotten many things that happened since. You must remember everything that happened on that day.

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Everything!

sp.speaker: The Lady.
sp.p: Do you remember a baby being received into the Foundling when you were first employed there?

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: I remember it well.

sp.speaker: The Lady.
sp.p: Is the child living?

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Living, and hearty, thank God!

sp.speaker: The Lady.
sp.p: Perhaps, you took care of him when he was a baby?

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: No, ma'am. The baby was sent to our institution in the country; and I was kept here to learn the ways of the house.

sp.speaker: The Lady.
sp.p: I have learnt the ways of the house, too. The baby was christened in the chapel here, before it was sent away to the country?

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Yes, ma'am. And I saw the christening.

sp.speaker: The Lady.
sp.p: They gave the child a name—a christian name and a surname. What was it?

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Don't ask me! We are not allowed to tell.

sp.speaker: The Lady.
sp.p: The child was my child! You must tell me!
Come back! come back! You may one day marry. As you hope to be a respected wife—as you hope to be a proud mother—as you are a living, loving woman, tell me the name!

div.stage: (Falls on her knees.)

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Don't, don't, ma'am! You are trying to make me do wrong!

sp.speaker: The Lady.
sp.p: Only his name, Sally! Only his name!

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Oh, dear! dear! I ought to say No—and I feel as if I was going to say Yes. Do let me go!

sp.speaker: The Lady.
sp.p: His name, Sally! His name!

sp.speaker: Sally
sp.p: Will you promise?

sp.speaker: The Lady
sp.p: Anything!

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Put your two hands in mine. Promise you will never ask me to tell you more than the christian name and surname which they gave to the child?

sp.speaker: The Lady.
sp.p: I promise!

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Walter Wilding.

div.stage: (The Lady embraces her in silence. The two go out at different sides of the stage. The scene changes.)

div.head: Second Scene.
div.stage: —The Boys' dining-room at the Foundling. The boys at dinner. A bright cheerful scene. Visitors —ladies and gentlemen—present, looking on. Among the visitors, The Lady. She passes down the table—which crosses the stage obliquely, and is lost to view behind the scene—looking anxiously at the boys one by one. Sally Goldstraw is among the nurses in attendance. The Lady keeps out of her way, and Sally is too busy to notice her. Two of the visitors, a husband and wife, come down to the front.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Mr. Jones, what do you mean by bringing me here?

sp.speaker: Husband.
sp.p: You wanted to come here, dear.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: I consider this place to be a sink of iniquity. How dare you to tell me I wanted to come to a sink of iniquity.

sp.speaker: Husband.
sp.p: It seems to be pretty cheerful for a sink, dear.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: When I think of the histories of these wretched children, I blush for human nature.

sp.speaker: Husband.
sp.p: Human nature ought to be much obliged to you, dear.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: A Foundling Hospital is an encouragement to vice. A man who brings his wife into a place which encourages vice, is a man lost to the commonest sense of decency. Give me your arm directly.

sp.speaker: Husband.
sp.p: Yes, dear.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Mr. Jones, you are a fool!

sp.speaker: Husband.
sp.p: Considering that I have married you, dear, perhaps you had better keep that opinion to yourself.

div.stage: (Exeunt.) (A second husband and wife come forward.)

sp.speaker: 2nd Wife.
sp.p: Mr. Brown, this is the most interesting sight I ever saw in my life. I should like to kiss every one of those boys.

sp.speaker: 2nd Husband.
sp.p: Think of our own boys, my dear. They wouldn't thank you for kissing them at dinner-time.

sp.speaker: 2nd Wife.
sp.p: I hope these poor little fellows are happy! It's so sad to think that they never knew a mother's love, and never climbed on a father's knee!

sp.speaker: 2nd Husband.
sp.p: Look at them, my dear! Our own boys couldn't eat a better dinner than that.

sp.speaker: 2nd Wife
sp.p: This is a noble charity! This is helping the helpless as Christians should.

sp.speaker: 2nd Husband.
sp.p: A noble charity, as you say. I have counted forty boys in this room, my dear, who are every one of them as fat as our Tom!

div.stage: (They walk up, and join the other visitors. In the vacant space left on the stage, Sally Goldstraw and The Lady suddenly meet.)

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: You here again! What did you promise me last night?

sp.speaker: The Lady.
sp.p: I said I would never ask you to tell me more than you told me then. I don't ask you to say another word. You can add to the debt of gratitude that I owe you, without speaking. Good Sally! Kind Sally! Show me my boy!

sp.speaker: Sally
sp.p: Oh, dear, dear! I'm going wrong again!

sp.speaker: The Lady.
sp.p: My heart is breaking, among all these children. Oh, think that my boy is here, and that I don't know him!

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Hush! not so loud. I am going to pass down the table. Follow me with your eyes. The boy that I stop and speak to, will not be your boy. But the boy that I touch will be Walter Wilding.

div.stage: (She passes down the table. Speaks to one boy, and touches the boy next to him, keeping her hand on his shoulder, and patting it. Both boys are seated with their backs to the audience. Sally, after lifting her hand from the boy, looks for the last time significantly at The Lady, and goes out, following the line of the table, which is lost to view behind the scenes. The Lady approaches the boy, and speaks to him.)

sp.speaker: The Lady
sp.p: How old are you?

sp.speaker: The Boy.
sp.p: I am twelve, ma'am.

sp.speaker: The Lady.
sp.p: Are you well and happy?

sp.speaker: The Boy.
sp.p: Yes, ma'am.

sp.speaker: The Lady.
sp.p: Would you like to be well provided for, and to be your own master when you grow up?

sp.speaker: The Boy.
sp.p: Yes, ma'am.

sp.speaker: The Lady.
sp.p: Would you like a home of your own? Would you like to find your mother who loves you?

sp.speaker: The Boy.
sp.p: Oh yes, ma'am, dearly!

div.stage: (The Lady kisses him, and turns away to hide her tears. At the same moment three strokes are heard on the end of the table hidden behind the scenes. A voice says, “Silence, for grace!” The boys all rise. The men among the visitors remove their hats. The grace is sung by boys' voices off the stage, to a simple hymn tune. At the last notes a double curtain closes slowly over the scene. On each division of the curtain is inscribed in large letters, visible to the whole audience: “TWELVE YEARS ELAPSE.” After a short interval, filled up by appropriate music, the curtain is withdrawn again, and the next scene opens on events which are supposed to occur, after the lapse of twelve years.)

div.head: Third Scene.
div.stage: —The Court-yard in the establishment of Wilding and Co., wine merchants, of Cripple Corner. A large counting-house with an open door, on one side. An entrance to the cellars, down steps. A large door in the flat, with a smaller door near it, various objects connected with the wine trade scattered about the yard. Walter Wilding, dressed in mourning, and Bintrey, discovered seated at a little table in the court-yard, with a bottle of wine between them.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Excuse my receiving you in the open air, Mr. Bintrey. What with the anxieties I have had lately, and what with the heat of the weather, I have been a good deal troubled with a giddiness in my head, and a singing in my ears.

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: And the fresh air clears your head, and quiets your ears? Just so, Mr. Walter Wilding—just so!

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Do you like this “forty-five,” sir?

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Like it? I am a lawyer. Did you ever hear of a lawyer who didn't like port? Capital wine, sir! In your place I shouldn't be quite so free in giving such wine away, even to my lawyer!

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: And now, as to my affairs, Mr. Bintrey. I think we have got everything straight. A partner secured.

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: A partner secured.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: A housekeeper advertised for—

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Housekeeper advertised for. “Apply personally at Cripple Corner, Great Tower-street, from ten to twelve—” to-day.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: My late dear mother's affairs wound up, and all charges paid—

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: And all charges paid. Without taxing the bill, which is the drollest professional circumstance I ever met with!
sp.stage: (Observes Wilding looking through the counting-house door, and looks that way too.)
sp.p: I see you have had the portrait of your mother hung in the counting-house?

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: My dear mother, as you know, placed me in this business, Mr. Bintrey. I have two portraits of her. One I keep in my own room. The other I hang in my counting-house, in remembrance of all that she has done for me. It seems like yesterday, when she came to the Foundling, and asked me if I should like to live in a home of my own, with the mother who loved me. From that time I became her confidentially acknowledged son. From that time, we were never separated till death took her from me, six months ago. Everything that I have—everything that may come to me in the future—I owe to her love. I hope my love consoled her for all that she had suffered in her earlier life. She had been cruelly deceived, Mr. Bintrey. But she never spoke of it—she never betrayed her betrayer!

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: She had made up her mind, and she could hold her peace. A devilish deal better than ever you will!

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: I can no longer show my love and honour for her; but I can show that I am not ashamed of her. I mean, that I am not ashamed of having been a Foundling. I, who never knew a father of my own, can be a father now to all in my employment. I shall expect my new partner, I shall expect my new housekeeper, to help me in keeping this resolution. We will revive the good old times, when the head of a business, and the clerks and servants of a business, all lived together as one family. I have told my people that they shall lodge here under the same roof with me, and eat here at the same table with me.

div.stage: (Joey Ladle appears, from the cellars.)

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Respecting this same boarding and lodging, young Master Wilding?

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Here is one of your new family.
sp.stage: (Pointing to Joey's leathern apron and bib.)
sp.p: This boy's pinasore won't want much washing, and won't wear out in a hurry!

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Well, Joey?

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Speaking for myself, young Master Wilding, if you want to board me and lodge me, take me. I can peck as well as most men. Where I peck, ain't so high a object with me as what I peck. And that ain't as high a object as how much I peck.

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: You ought to have been a lawyer, Mr. Joey. Where we peck isn't as high an object with us as what we peck, and how much we peck. Victuals in your case, and fees in ours. Human nature is the same in all professions, Mr. Wilding. I'll take another glass of the forty-five port.

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Are we all to live in the house, young Master Wilding? The two other cellarmen, the three porters, the two 'prentices, and the odd men?

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Yes, Joey. I hope we shall all be an united family.

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Ah! I hope they may be.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: They? Rather say we, Joey.

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Don't look to me to make “We” on it, young Master Wilding. Don't look to me to put a lively face on anything. It's all very well, gentlemen, for you that has been accustomed to take your wine into your systems by the convivial channel of your throttles, to put a lively face on it. But I have been accustomed to take my wine in at the pores of the skin—and, took that way, it acts depressing. It's one thing to charge your glasses in a dining-room with a Hip—Hip—Hooray, and a Jolly Companions Everyone. And its another thing to be charged yourself, through the pores, in a low dark cellar and a mouldy atmosphere. I have been a cellarman my life through—and what's the consequence? I'm as muddled and as molloncolly a man as lives. A pecking-machine, sir, is all that I am capable of proving myself, out of my cellars. But that you're welcome to, if it's worth your while to keep such a thing on your premises.

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: I don't want to interrupt the flow of Mr. Joey's philosophy. But it's past ten o'clock—and the housekeepers will be coming to apply for the vacant place.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Let them come, and welcome. My good friend, George Vendale, has undertaken to see them for me, and to pick out the woman whom he thinks will suit me best.
sp.stage: (Bintrey nods, and turns to go out.)
sp.p: You're not going?

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: I have an appointment in court. I'll look in on my way back, and hear what you have done.

div.stage: (Exit.)

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: So, you've been and taken young Master George Vendale partner into the old business?

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Yes, Joey. My old friend George Vendale begins, as my partner, to-day.

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Don't change the name of the Firm again, young Master Wilding. It was bad luck enough to make it Yourself and Co. Better by far have left the old name of the old Firm—Pebbleson Nephew. Good luck always stuck to Pebbleson Nephew. You should never change luck when it's good, sir.

div.stage: Enter George Vendale, from the house.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I have seen the housekeepers, Walter. There is only one woman in the whole collection who isn't a Gorgon. I like her face and her manner—and she is coming here to be presented to you. Her name is Sarah Goldstraw.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Goldstraw! Surely I have heard that name before?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: If she is an old acquaintance, so much the better
This way, Miss Goldstraw. Here is Mr. Wilding!

div.stage: Enter Sally Goldstraw.

sp.speaker: Sally
sp.p: Wilding!

sp.speaker: Joey
sp.p: I agree with Master George. That's a sound woman, outside and in!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: This is a busy morning with me. I am going to the Docks—then back again to the house, to speak to the gas-fitter about the new light in the dining-room. Good-bye, for the present!

div.stage: (Exit through the counting-house.)

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Will you step into the counting-house, if you please?
Her face is familiar to me! Where did I see it last?

sp.speaker: Sally
sp.stage: (advancing a few steps, and stopping thoughtfully).
sp.p: Wilding!—No, no, it can't be? Wilding's a common name. How foolish I am!

sp.speaker: Joey
sp.p: Take her, young Master Wilding! You won't find the match of Sarah Goldstraw in a hurry.
I feel as if I had taken something new in at the pores.
Has that pleasant woman brought a streak of sunshine with her into this molloncolly place? And am I a-walking in it on my way back to the cellars?

div.stage: (Exit into the cellars.)

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Let me show you the way into the counting-house.

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: I beg your pardon, sir.

div.stage: (She goes on to the counting-house—and is about to enter the door, when she suddenly starts back with a scream, and sinks on a bench in the yard.)

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: What's the matter? what have you seen to frighten you?

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Nothing!

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Nothing?

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Might I ask—? there's a portrait in the counting-house, sir—

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: The portrait of my late mother. What is there in that to frighten you?

sp.speaker: Sally
sp.p: His mother. The lady who spoke to me twelve years since!
I hope you will excuse me, sir, I would rather not take up your time. I—I don't think the place would suit me.

div.stage: (Attempts to retire.)

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Wait a minute. There's something wrong here—there's something I don't understand. Your face puzzles me; your name puzzles me—good Heavens! I have it! You were the nurse at the Foundling, when I was one of the boys there twelve years since!

sp.speaker: Sally
sp.p: What am I to say to him?

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: You were the woman who took pity on my poor mother. She often talked of it to me. A nurse told her my name, and pointed me out to her at dinner. You were that nurse.

sp.speaker: Sally
sp.p: Heaven forgive me, sir, I was that nurse!

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Heaven forgive you? What do you mean? Speak out!

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Oh, sir, don't ask me to speak out! I may make you rue the day when you first let me into your house.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: You can do nothing worse than frighten me as you are frightening me now.

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Compose yourself, sir! If I must speak, I will. You said a minute since that the lady—

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: She calls my mother “the lady!” When you talk of my mother, why don't you call her my mother?

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: You said just now, sir, that the lady often talked of what had passed between herself and me. Are you calm enough to remember what she told you?

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Calm or not, it is impossible that I can forget it. You told my mother that you were present when I was first received at the Foundling. You saw me christened; you heard me named Walter Wilding. You said that I was removed to the institution in the country, and that you remained at the institution in London.

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: All quite true then, sir—and all quite true now. But you don't know—and at that time, I didn't know either—what happened at our place in the country. A strange lady—one Mrs. Miller—came there, six months after the child had been removed from London. Her object was to adopt one of our foundlings; and she was provided with the necessary authority. The child she chose, was the infant whom I had seen christened—the child of the lady whose portrait hangs there.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Why can't you speak plainly? You mean me?

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: I mean the child of that lady, sir. You are not her child.

You were not received into the Foundling until three weeks after the date I am speaking of. I was absent at the time—or this would never have happened. You, in your turn, were christened at the chapel in London. There was a question of what name to give you. The name of the child who had been taken away from us, was a name to spare—and it was given to you. You, too, were taken to the country. At three years old you were brought back to the London Foundling. I was ignorant of all the circumstances. What could I conclude, when you came back to us, under the name of Walter Wilding, but that you were the child whom I had seen christened by that name? How could I know that there had been a first Walter Wilding, adopted, and taken away, and a second Walter Wilding put in his place?

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Is it getting dark? Are my eyes failing me? Give me a hand—I don't know where I am.

sp.speaker: Sally
sp.stage: (supporting him, and placing him on the bench from which she has risen).
sp.p: Shall I get you some water, sir? Shall I call for help?

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Wait—give me time.
How do I know your story is true?

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Should I have told it, sir, in my situation, if it had not been true?

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Oh me! oh me! I loved her so dearly! I felt so fondly I was her son!

div.stage: (His head sinks. Sally kneels by him and supports it on her bosom.)

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Let it rest here, sir. This is not the first time. I have rocked you to sleep, on my bosom, many and many a time when you were a boy.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: She died, Sally, in my arms—she died blessing me as only a mother could have blessed me. Oh, if you were to speak—Why not have spoken sooner?

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: I only knew it myself, sir, two years since, I found the work at the Foundling too much for me, and left to take a housekeeper's situation. I went to say goodbye to a friend at our place in the country, and there I heard it for the first time. Where was I to find the poor lady? Where was I to find you? It's not my fault, sir. If you hadn't forced me to it, I wouldn't have spoken now.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: What! you would have left me ignorant of the truth? You would have left me usurping the place, enjoying the fortune that belongs to another man? He must be found! Who was the stranger who adopted the child?

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: The lady's name was Mrs. Miller, sir.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Where is she?

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: It's nigh on four-and-twenty years since, sir. All that is known of her is, that she took the child to Switzerland.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Switzerland? What part of Switzerland?

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Nobody heard at the time, sir; and nobody knows now.

div.stage: Enter Bintrey.

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Well? Have you engaged the housekeeper?
What's the matter?

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Tell him, in your own words—I can't tell him in any words of mine!
sp.stage: (Sally and Bintrey speak apart. Wilding continues, in soliloquy.)
sp.p: She left me her fortune—she left me all that I possess, in the firm persuasion that I was her son. I am not her son. I have got the place, I have innocently taken the inheritance of another man. He must be found, Mr. Bintrey!

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Wait in the house a little, and let me speak to him.
sp.stage: (Sally goes into the house. Bintrey turns and addresses Wilding.)
sp.p: This is a sad business, Mr. Wilding. But I can't see that Sarah Goldstraw is to blame.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: To blame? She's a good kind woman, and she shall stop here, in my service. Never mind that now! Mr. Bintrey, the lost Walter Wilding must be found!

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: After a lapse of four-and-twenty years? Not easy, to say the least of it.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: I tell you her son must be found. It may take time; I may die before it's done—Stop! I must make my will—a will leaving everything to him—before I sleep to-night.

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Gently! gently!

div.stage: Enter George Vendale from the house.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Oh, George, you come at a terrible time! You don't know what has happened!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: My dear Walter! the woman herself has told me. I saw her here on my return from the Docks, and she entreated me, as your old friend, to go and comfort you.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Encourage me, George! Take my side. I am determined to find the lost man, and to restore everything to him—for her sake, and for the love I bear to her memory.

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: How are we to find the man, Mr. Vendale? If we advertise for him, we invite every rogue in the kingdom to set up a claim. Taking our friend's own view— which I, for one, don't share—this restitution is impossible. Try what way you please, Mr. Wilding, you will find this is a case of No Thoroughfare!

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: The restitution must, and shall, be made! I have got what belongs to another man. I am an Impostor!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: My good friend, that is simply absurd. No man can be an impostor without being a consenting party to the imposition. Clearly, you never were that. As to your enrichment by the lady whom you believed to be your mother, it arose out of the personal relations between you —out of the pure love she had for you, out of the pure love you had for her. A mistake for which you were neither of you responsible, can't alter that.

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Besides, the man may be dead.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: The man may be living! We know that the child was taken to Switzerland. That is the clue to follow. If neither of you will help me, I will go to Switzerland myself!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Hush! hush! You know we will both help you to any object that you really have at heart. Compose yourself, Walter; we will return to this painful subject later in the day.

div.stage: Enter Joey.

sp.speaker: Joey
sp.p: A gentleman has stopped at the door, sir, in a cab. He wishes to see you.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Who is he?

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: A stranger, sir. Here is his card, and a letter.

div.stage: (Joey withdraws and waits at the back.)

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: See who it is! I can't receive anybody.

div.stage: (Hands Vendale the card and letter.)

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: “Mr. Obenreizer!”

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.stage: (looking over Vendale's shoulder at the card).
sp.p: From Switzerland.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Switzerland! Whoever he is, I'll see him.

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: You have changed your mind rather suddenly.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: The one trace of the lost man is in Switzerland. Even this stranger may help us.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Mr. Obenreizer is not a stranger. He was an old acquaintance of mine, when I was travelling abroad. This letter is from our correspondents—Defresnier and Company, the wine-merchants of Neuchâtel. They introduce Mr. Obenreizer as Agent for their house, and as now intending to establish himself in England. And they recommend him warmly to the friendly consideration of Wilding and Company.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: What sort of a man is he? How is it you never mentioned him before?

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Mr. Vendale looks confused. That's a bad sign to begin with!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I had my reasons, Walter. When Mr. Obenreizer and I first met abroad there was somebody with him. In plain English, there was a young lady—

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: His daughter?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: He is no older than you and I.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: No older than I am!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: No older. The young lady was his ward; and—

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: And you fell in love with her? Excuse my legal habit of helping an unwilling witness.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I'm not an unwilling witness in that part of the matter. I have been in love with her ever since—I am in love with her now—I shall be in love with her to the end of my life. Is that sufficiently explicit, Mr. Bintrey?

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: I can't say, Mr. Vendale. I'm not professionally acquainted with the subject.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: I don't see what tied your tongue about all this, George—so far.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: The truth is, I was very young at the time, and very anxious to make an impression on the young lady. I drifted into some foolish boasting about myself and my family position. I have had sense enough to be ashamed of it since, and Mr. Obenreizer's arrival makes me feel doubly ashamed of it now.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Do you object to see him?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Certainly not! We are to be connected with him in business. Let us get the meeting over; and the sooner the better.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: As Mr. Obenreizer to step this way.

div.stage: (Joey opens the door of the house, and Obenreizer appears. Joey goes out.)

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Mr. Walter Wilding?

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: My name is Wilding, sir. You come excellently introduced. I am glad to see you.
My friend, and legal adviser—Mr. Bintrey.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Charmed to make Mr. Bintrey's acquaintance.

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Too civil by half! I don't like him.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Ha! my fellow-traveller, Mr. Vendale! How do you do? So glad!
sp.stage: (Takes Vendale lightly by each elbow, by way of embrace.)

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: You hardly expected to meet me again here, as a partner in the firm?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: On the contrary! I heard at Neuchâtel you had become a member of the firm. Besides, what did I tell you when we were on the mountains? We call them vast—but the world is so little! So little is the world that one cannot keep away from persons. Does one wish to keep away from you? Good Heavens, no! And you are quite well? So glad!

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: He has rather a tigerish way of being glad!

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Charmed with Mr. Obenriezer's sentiments—that's all!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: And you have had the condescension to come into trade? You, descended from so fine a family! A dealer in wines! Stop, though! Wine? Is it trade in England, or profession? Not a fine art?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Mr. Obenreizer, when we last met, I had only come of age—I was young and foolish; and I had just inherited the fortune left to me after my parents' death. I have grown a year or two older, and I have got rid of my boy's vanity, since that time.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Your vanity? Bah! You tax yourself too heavily—you tax yourself as if it was your Government taxing you! My dear sir, I like your condescension. It ennobles trade! The misfortune of trade, is its vulgarity. Any low people—I, for example, a poor peasant—may take to it, and climb by it. Yes, Mr. Wilding! Yes, Mr. Bintrey! I possess your English virtue of frankness. I own myself a man of low origin—bah! for all I know, a man of no origin at all!

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Do you hear that?

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: I'm deaf, on principle, to all humbug!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: May I ask after your ward! Is Mademoiselle Marguerite well?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.stage: (suddenly altering in manner, and speaking feelingly and seriously).
sp.p: Mademoiselle Marguerite is, I am happy to say, sir, quite well!

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: You are rather young, Mr. Obenreizer, to be a lady's guardian.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Young in years, Mr. Bintrey; old in discretion and experience. The father of this young lady —whom it is the honour and the happiness of my life to protect—was, by origin, a peasant like myself. He had watched me from my childhood—he had seen me win my way honestly, inch by inch, higher in the world, as he had won his. He died, a lonely man who had outlived all the friends of his own time—he died, knowing that he could trust me. I received his priceless charge—the charge of his child. At my request, her little fortune was secured to her, independently of me, when she comes of age. I only accepted the small yearly sum which her father left to me, on that understanding. I shall live and die true to my sacred trust!

Mr. Wilding! you are asked to put confidence in me in matters of trade. I am not sure of my origin—I am not even sure if my parents were my parents after all. But one thing I know! I must be open as the day; I must be true as steel—or my friend's daughter would never have been trusted to these peasant's hands!

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: He is about my age—he is not sure of his origin; he is not sure of his parents. You hear him again?

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: No, I don't hear him again!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Is Mademoiselle Marguerite in Switzerland?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Mademoiselle Marguerite is here. With her excellent relative, Madame Dor.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Do you mean that the ladies are waiting for you?
Beg them to join us directly! I am shocked to think that ladies should have been kept waiting at my door. I'll go and fetch them myself!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Not for the world!

div.stage: (Exit.)

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I shall see her again! Oh, if she only remembers me as I remember her!

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: I must ask him about his early life. There may be something providential in the accident which has brought this man here to-day!

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Mr. Wilding, when Mr. Obenreizer comes back, will you favour me by doing something?

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Certainly! What can I do?

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: If you choose to make a great effort, you can hold your tongue!

div.stage: (Enter Obenreizer, leading in Marguerite, and followed by Madame Dor. Madame Dor has a dirty glove on one hand, which she is cleaning with india-rubber. Sitting or standing she always keeps her back turned on the persons about her)

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: My ward—Mademoiselle Marguerite!
sp.stage: (Wilding and Bintrey bow. Marguerite notices Vendale, betrays her pleasure at meeting him again, then glances at Obenreizer, and suddenly restrains herself. She and Vendale talk apart. Meanwhile Obenreizer, in his jesting tone, introduces Madame Dor.)
sp.p: Madame Dor! the guardian angel, gentlemen, of my gloves and stockings!
sp.stage: (Madame D. bobs sideways to Wilding and Bintrey, and plumps down, with her back to everybody, cleaning the glove. Obenreizer continues.)
sp.p: You adore domestic details in this country, Mr. Wilding! You insist on nothing else in your books; you will buy nothing else in your pictures. Behold

the most domestic woman in existence! To-day, she is cleaning my gloves; to-morrow she will be darning my stockings; the day after she will be up to her elbows in suet and flour, making my puddings—my good, solid, indigestible English puddings! You admire her fine large back, don't you? Bah! her back is a baby, compared to her heart!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Have you ever thought since of our happy days in Switzerland?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Over and over again, Mr. Vendale. Do you remember our lakes and mountains?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I only remember you!

div.stage: (Marguerite turns aside confused.)

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: I am afraid the journey has fatigued you? I am afraid all these new faces here confuse you.
sp.stage: (Marguerite makes a sign in the negative.)
sp.p: No? Ah! you are too kind to let me be anxious about you! You will acknowledge nothing that can give me a moment's pain!
sp.stage: (She passes on to Wilding and Bintrey, who speak to her apart. Obenreizer turns abruptly to Vendale.)
sp.p: Ha! Mr. Vendale, I will make that charming creature's English home, a home that is worthy of her! Where the money is to come from, who knows? But it shall be done! Silks, and satins, and laces, and flowers— my ward shall have them all. Can your sound English sense understand a man who sacrifices everything to one dominant idea? I dare say not! You are so well brought up in England; you are so prosperous and so rich! I was brought up in the cowshed with the cow! I was brought up barefooted, to beg for halfpence on the highway! While your parents were saying to you, “Nice boy, come and kiss us!” my parents (if they were my parents) were saying to me, “Little wretch! come and have the stick!”
sp.stage: (Wilding makes an attempt to speak to Obenreizer. Bintrey holds him back.)
sp.p: Bah! we were a sordid set where I passed my young life. I wish I could forget Switzerland.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: For my part, I love Switzerland.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Then, I love it too! I have said nothing to hurt you, I hope? A slip of the tongue, dearest! Remember that we are speaking in proud England!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: I speak in proud earnest. I am not ashamed of my country—I am not ashamed of being a peasant's daughter.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I understand your feeling, and admire it.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.stage: (to Marguerite, after looking at his watch).
sp.p: I am sure you are fatigued! I am sure you need rest and quiet! En route, my dear Marguerite! en route, my good Dor! Mr. Wilding, I am delighted to have presented myself.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Mr. Obenreizer—

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Hold your tongue!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: We must be firm friends— we must do business together—we must exchange hospitalities when I have a home of my own. I am eager for your English puddings! I adore your glorious grogs!
sp.stage: (Turns away, and rouses Madame Dor. Bintrey persists in silencing Wilding.)

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: When shall we meet again?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: It depends on Mr. Obenreizer!

div.stage: (She joins Obenreizer.)

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Adieu, gentlemen, for the present! Mr. Wilding, you shall hear from me to-morrow.
Now, dearest, for our house-hunting in this great city! We will find you the prettiest home to live in that London can produce!

div.stage: (He goes out with Marguerite. Madame Dor follows sideways, still cleaning the glove. At the same moment, Vendale and Bintrey, at either side of the stage, and Wilding in the middle, all three turn towards the audience, each speaking in turn, in a whisper to himself.)

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: He is the kindest of guardians!

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: He is the greatest of rascals!

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: He may be the lost man!

div.head: First Scene.
div.stage: —The drawing-room at Obenreizer's lodgings. The room is richly furnished. On one side of the stage, Marguerite, elegantly dressed, stands at a window, looking out. On the other side, Obenreizer is engaged at an open desk, counting and arranging a sum of money in gold and bank-notes. In the centre, at the back of the stage, Madame Dor sits, with her back to the audience, cleaning a glove. A lapse of three months is supposed to have occurred since the First Act.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Mr. Vendale knows that to-day is my birthday—and yet Mr. Vendale never comes near me!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: One hundred, two hundred, four hundred—four hundred and fifty. Fifty pounds still wanting to make up the five hundred—the sum which I must replace—or I am a lost man! Oh, this ruinous luxury! this hollow show of prosperity and wealth! Will Marguerite ever know what the splendour she lives in has cost me? We have been three months in England. Have I produced no impression on her by all that I have done in that time? I must have produced an impression! She has been more familiar—there has been something almost affectionate in her manner to me lately. She thinks less—she evidently thinks less of that man, Vendale.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: No signs of Mr. Vendale! And yet I felt so sure that he would come to me on my birthday!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Vendale knows that it is her birthday. If he sends her a present, it will be the most brilliant present that wealth can buy. What am I going to give her? Nothing but the flowers that she loves!—the flowers whose eloquence I trust to speak for me. If I only dared use this money, I know whose birthday gift should be the richest! I have a month before me—the five hundred pounds won't be wanted for another month. Dare I run the risk? Madness to think of it! Every farthing I can spare must be scraped together to make up the missing sum. Discovery brands me as a felon—discovery ruins me for life. I'll lock the money up—the sight of it tempts me. Vendale? Bah! he is overwhelmed with business—he will forget her birthday.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Ah! I didn't reckon on him in vain. There he is in the street!
Mr. Vendale is coming!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: He has remembered the birthday! Come what may of it, Vendale shall not get the upper hand of me now!
Come in!

div.stage: Enter Vendale, with a jeweller's case in his hand. He bows to Obenreizer, and passes on to Marguerite.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: May I offer you my best wishes and congratulations? Will you honour me by accepting a little memorial of this happy day?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: A little memorial! Oh, Mr. Vendale! how modestly wealth speaks, when it speaks in England!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: You are very kind—I am much obliged to you, Mr. Vendale.
I hope he has remembered that a simple present is the only present I can accept from him!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: You don't open the case? Will you favour me by looking at what is inside?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: I can bear it no longer!
sp.stage: (Snatching the money out of the drawer.)
sp.p: The die is cast!
Excuse me, dearest, for one moment. Mr. Vendale reminds me that my birthday present has not been made yet!
sp.stage: (Goes out, stopping for a moment to speak to Madame Dor, and to show by a gesture that he desires her not to leave Vendale and Marguerite alone in his absence.)

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.stage: (opening the case, and taking from it a plain gold locket and chain).
sp.p: Oh, Mr. Vendale! how well you have understood me! A present that I might have received from a person in my own rank of life!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Is my little offering forgiven, as well as accepted?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: More than forgiven! I own you have pleased and flattered me!
sp.stage: (She places the locket in the bosom of her dress, and seats herself on the sofa.)

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Madame Dor! Is there no way of getting that piece of human furniture out of the room? Stay! Her head nods—her stocking falls into her lap. Best of women! yield to Nature's weakness, and mercifully fall asleep!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.stage: (noticing Madame Dor, and rising to wake her).
sp.p: Madame Dor!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.stage: (taking Marguerite's hand, and leading her back to the sofa).
sp.p: Don't disturb her! I have been waiting to tell you a secret, which must be heard by nobody but ourselves. Let me tell it now!

div.stage: (He seats himself by Marguerite on the sofa. She takes up her embroidery, and tries to hide her confusion, by affecting to work.)

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: What claim can I have, Mr. Vendale, to know your secrets?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I can never tell you, if you persist in looking at your work.

We have often talked of those delightful days in Switzerland, when we were fellow-travellers. I have often told you of the impressions I brought back with me to England. But there is one impression that I have never mentioned yet. Can you guess what that one is?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: I am very bad at guessing, Mr. Vendale. It was an impression of the mountains, perhaps?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: No: a much more precious impression than that.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: An impression of the lakes?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: No. The lakes are not associated with my happiness in the present, and my hopes in the future. Marguerite! all that makes life worth having, hangs for me on a word from your lips. Marguerite! I love you!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Oh, Mr. Vendale, it would have been kinder to have kept your secret! Have you forgotten the distance between us? It can never, never be!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: There can be but one distance between us—a distance of your making. My love! there is no higher rank in goodness, there is no higher rank in beauty, than yours! Come! whisper the one little word! Tell me you will be my wife!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Think of your family! and think of mine!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: If you dwell on such an obstacle as that, I shall think but one thought—I shall think I have offended you.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Oh no!
sp.stage: (She stops, confused, and tries to disengage herself.)
sp.p: I didn't mean that! I—I don't know what I mean! Let me go, Mr. Vendale!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Call me George!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: George!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Say you love me!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.stage: (timidly touching his cheek with her lips).
sp.p: I love you!
sp.stage: (A pause. Footsteps heard outside. Marguerite starts to her feet.)
sp.p: Leave me! He is coming back!

div.stage: (Madame Dor wakes with a start. She drops several old gloves, which all roll off her lap together. Vendale hurries to the back to pick them up for her. Marguerite stands looking towards the door, uncertain whether to go or stay. Obenreizer appears, radiant with triumph. He has a jeweller's case in his hand, and is followed by two men, who place pots of rare flowers, under his directions, in different parts of the room.)

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Look, dearest, at the flowers— and tell me if one of your favourites has been forgotten!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: You are too kind! How can I thank you?

div.stage: (She takes Vendale's locket nervously out of her dress.)

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: My birthday present is not made yet! You are pleased with the flowers; but the flowers will wither with time. I have another and a better gift, which will always remind you of me. Marguerite! I have inherited no fortune from my parents. All that I possess I owe to my own exertions—and that little “all” I offer to you.
Wear these, dearest, and give them a beauty which is not their own!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.stage: (opening the case, and taking out a diamond necklace).
sp.p: Oh! how could you buy this! How can a girl like me wear such diamonds as these? You will not be offended? I do wish you had been satisfied with only giving me the flowers!
sp.stage: (She has spoken these words—feeling Obenreizer's eyes fixed eagerly on her—timidly and with embarrassment. She places the necklace on the table, mechanically arranges Vendale's locket round her neck, suddenly realises the effect of what she is doing on Obenreizer, starts, and turns away abruptly to Madame Dor.)
sp.p: Madame Dor! it's getting late! Come and help me to dress for dinner.

div.stage: (She hurries out, taking Madame Dor with her. Vendale remains at the back, looking after her.)

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: His locket round her neck, and my necklace left on the table! I have risked the horrors of discovery—I have sacrificed my honour—I have put my whole future in peril to win her love—and this is my reward! Curses on your glitter and your beauty! You have ruined me for life!

div.stage: (He snatches up the diamonds, and throws them from him in a frenzy of rage. The moment after, Vendale approaches him with both hands extended cordially.)

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: My dear friend, I have something to say to you!
sp.stage: (A stifled cry of fury and a threatening gesture escape Obenreizer. He controls himself the moment after, and, without taking Vendale's outstretched hands, points to a chair. Vendale continues.)
sp.p: What is the matter? Has anything happened to annoy you?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: My nerves are out of order. I'm not quite myself to-day. Don't notice! You want to speak to me. Take a seat. This is business, I suppose?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.stage: (seating himself, with a look of surprise).
sp.p: Business! Something much more interesting than business. I am afraid you are hardly well enough—?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: I am quite well enough. What is it?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Mr. Obenreizer, you must have observed, long since, that I feel no ordinary admiration for your charming ward.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: I have not observed it.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: My admiration has grown into a tenderer and deeper feeling—

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Friendship, Mr. Vendale?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Love.
sp.stage: (Obenreizer starts to his feet. Vendale continues.)
sp.p: I appear to surprise you?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: You—!
sp.stage: (Masters himself by a great effort, and resumes his chair.)
sp.p: You petrify me.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Shall I wait till you have recovered yourself?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: No!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: You wish me to go on?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Yes!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: You are Mademoiselle Marguerite's guardian. I ask you to confer upon me the greatest of all favours—I ask you to give me her hand in marriage.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: You ask me—!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I beg your pardon?—I didn't hear—

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: One word, sir. You have said nothing about this to the young lady herself?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I have opened my whole heart to the young lady.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Mr. Vendale—!
Mr. Vendale, what sort of conduct is this? As a man of honour speaking to a man of honour, how can you justify it?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: The customs of your country and mine differ. Why do you receive my proposals in this strange way? What objection do you see to favouring my suit?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: I see one immense objection. My ward is the daughter of a peasant, and you are the son of a gentleman. In this country, such a marriage as you propose is an outrage on society.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Mr. Obenreizer, I may claim to know my own country better than you do. In the estimation of everybody whose opinion is worth having, my wife herself would be the one sufficient justification of my marriage. In offering her my love, I know that I am also offering her the respect of all my friends. I am not so rich as you suppose me to be; but I can give my wife a home and a position that are worthy of her. My present income is fifteen hundred a year, and I have the fairest prospect of soon making it more. Do you object to me on pecuniary grounds?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Yes!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Because you are not rich enough.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I have just told you that I have fifteen hundred a year!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Enough, I dare say, for an English wife in your own station. Not more than half enough for a foreign wife, who has all your social prejudices to conquer. Answer me this. On your fifteen hundred a year, can your wife have a house in a fashionable quarter, a footman to open her door, a butler to wait at her table, and a carriage and horses to drive about in? Yes? or No?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: No!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: One more question, and I have done. Take the mass of your lovely and accomplished countrywomen. Is it, or is it not, the fact, that a lady who has a house in a fashionable quarter, a footman to open her door, a butler to wait at her table, and a carriage and horses to drive about in—is a lady who has gained four steps in female estimation, at starting?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: He has betrayed himself at last. The mercenary motive is at the bottom of it all!
You view this question as a question of terms?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Of terms beyond your reach.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: On your own showing, you could offer no valid objection to my proposal, if I had three thousand a year. I shall have a word to say to you presently about that part of the question. But I will wait till you have consulted the wishes of Mademoiselle Marguerite, first.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: What has she to do with this discussion?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: She has the same interest in it that I have.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: What do you mean?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I have had the assurance from her own lips that she loves me.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.stage: (furiously striking the bell on the table).
sp.p: We'll see about that!
Mademoiselle Marguerite!
sp.stage: (The Servant retires. Marguerite enters. Obenreizer looks at her as she slowly advances towards him.)
sp.p: Her colour is rising! How lovely she looks!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: You wish to speak to me?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Yes, dearest. I have something to say to you, at the request of this gentleman. Mr. Vendale asserts—

div.stage: (His voice falters; he turns aside abruptly.)

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: You look worn and anxious. Are you ill? I am so sorry!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: She pities me! The angel looks down and pities me!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Have I said anything to distress you?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: You have turned the knife in the wound—that's all! No! no! no! I don't mean that— I mean nothing! We are forgetting Mr. Vendale. Marguerite! He has said—
—he has said that you love him.
It is not true—is it?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: It is true!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Damnation!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: How strangely he looks!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Are you satisfied now?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Wait a little!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: He frightens me!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: A word more—a little word more, dearest, between us. You know that I alone have authority over you as your guardian?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.stage: (fearing a dispute between the two men).
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: If Mr. Vendale is ever to marry you, it must be with my consent?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: You promise to be guided in this matter by my regard for your welfare, and by my better knowledge of the world?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: If I say wait—whatever Mr. Vendale may say— you will wait my time?

div.stage: (Vendale attempts to interpose. Marguerite, in terror of what may happen, silences him by a gesture.)

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: You will wait my time?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Mr. Vendale, are you answered?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I am not answered. You have heard from herself that she loves me. In her presence, I tell you again that I love her. In her presence, state your objection to me. I repeat my proposal.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: I decline your proposal.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: On what ground?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: On the ground of your income.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Fifteen hundred a year, is—in your opinion—not enough?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Not more than half enough!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: That is your objection?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: That is my objection.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I take you at your word. Mr. Obenreizer! I will double my income.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Easier said than done!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Watch the course of my business for another year, and you will see it done.—Marguerite! will you wait for me?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Willingly, Geor—!
sp.stage: (Sees Obenreizer looking at her, and corrects herself.)
sp.p: Yes, Mr. Vendale!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: In a year more, you shall be my wife!

div.stage: (He turns towards the door.)

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: George!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Marguerite!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.stage: (looking at him with a cry of terror).
sp.p: Oh!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: You have frightened her!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Have I frightened you?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: I was a little startled—that's all!

div.stage: (She looks at Vendale. He attempts to approach her. Obenreizer places himself between them).

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: No, Mr. Vendale. You are not her husband yet!

div.stage: (The Scene closes on them.)

div.head: Second Scene.
div.stage: —A room in Wilding's house. Side entrances, right and left. A door in the flat scene. Bintrey enters from the side, and knocks at the door in the flat. It is opened by Sally Goldstraw, who closes it behind her before she speaks to Bintrey.

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Did you wish to see Mr. Wilding, sir?

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Yes. I have been away a week on business, and I want to ask him how he does.

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: You can't see him now, sir. He has promised me to lie down, and try if he can get a little sleep. The new doctor warned me not to let him be disturbed.

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: What, another doctor called in! When I was here last, Mr. Wilding was able to walk and talk. All he complained of was the oppression in his head. You don't mean to say he is dangerously ill?

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: He is able to walk and talk still, sir. But I am afraid he is dangerously ill, for all that. Three days since he alarmed us dreadfully—he had a fit. The doctors say that a second attack will be the death of him. I have my orders not to let him be vexed or disturbed. And, to own the truth, sir, I am afraid he would be both vexed and disturbed, if he saw you.

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Come! that's plain speaking, at any rate. What have I done to upset him, if you please?

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: He can't rest night or day, sir, for thinking of the lost Walter Wilding. And he blames you for stopping his inquiries, when he wanted to make them, and when he had health and strength to do it.

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: My good woman! you have your duty towards Mr. Wilding; and I have mine. My duty is to keep my old friend and client from being swindled by the first rogue who chooses to impose on him.
Obenreizer, for example!

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Still, you might humour him, sir, mightn't you? He does take it, Mr. Bintrey, so much to heart!

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: I have humoured him—I have drawn his will. And what's more, I have let him execute it. The most absurd document that ever was put on paper! Mr. Vendale and I are charged, as his executors, to find a lost man, without knowing where to look for him—and to give that man a fortune, no matter who or what he may be, if he ever turns up! In drawing that will, I have committed professional suicide—and here's a worthy woman who tells me I hav'n't humoured my client!

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: I'm sure you mean well, sir! But he's so anxious and so ill—and I am so sorry for him! In old days at the Foundling, I used to call him “my boy.” And somehow—I can't explain it—he seems to be growing back, in this distress of his, to be “my boy” again!

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: You may be old enough to be his mother, Miss Goldstraw—but you don't look it, at any rate!

sp.speaker: Sally
sp.p: Thank you, sir!

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Don't mention it! Come! come! I see you think I may be of some use in quieting poor Wilding's mind. What can I do?

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Help him, sir, to find the lost man.

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Help him to find somebody who will relieve him of every farthing he has in the world! If I do, I'll be—

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Hush, sir! I don't think you understand poor Mr. Wilding's case. He is not to be reasoned with in this matter. It will be the death of him if his present anxiety is not relieved.

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Was there ever such perversity? A man dying with anxiety to see another man make a pauper of him! —There! there! I'll tell you what I'll do—I'll help him, but it must be on my own terms. If the lost man is to be found (the devil take him!), it's my address he shall apply at, and not Wilding's. If he gets half the fortune out of me, he may think himself lucky! I hate the fellow by anticipation! Tell Mr. Wilding I'll make inquiries— and say, I'll call and report to-morrow. Will that pacify him?

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: I'm sure it will, sir. Ah, you may be rough outside, Mr. Bintrey—but you have a good heart.

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Don't take away my character, Miss Goldstraw!

div.stage: (Exit.)

sp.speaker: Sally
sp.p: It's no laughing matter, Mr. Bintrey. If something isn't done to quiet his mind, I tremble to think of what may happen before long!

div.stage: (Wilding enters by the door in the flat. He is clothed in his dressing-gown. His manner expresses mental, rather than physical, weakness.)

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Did I hear Mr. Bintrey?

sp.speaker: Sally
sp.p: Oh, sir! I am afraid we have disturbed you.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: You have not disturbed me. I can't rest; I can't compose myself. Every day I live, I am doing a new injustice to the man whose place I have taken, whose fortune I have got. Nobody helps me—nobody tries to find him!

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Mr. Bintrey will try, sir. He told me to say so, a minute since.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Mr. Bintrey will put it off—Mr. Bintrey doesn't see this as I see it—Mr. Bintrey suspects people, without reason.
Obenreizer is the man! I think of it by day; I dream of it by night; and all my thoughts and all my dreams point the same way—Obenreizer is her son!
Sally!—may I call you Sally, for the sake of old times, when I was a boy?

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Oh yes, sir! Try and be like what you were in the old times. You were always patient when you were a boy. Try and be patient now!

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Yes! yes! Something happened to me, Sally, a day or two since. Did I faint? Or—was it a fit? Tell me —I want to know!

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: It was a fit, sir.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Ah! and there was a strange feeling in my head before it came on. Is it coming again? Sally! There is somebody whom I want to see—somebody whom I must see, before the day is out.

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Not now, sir! Wait till you are stronger!

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: My time may be short. I must, and will, speak to Obenreizer!
Where is Mr. Vendale?

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: He left word, I think, sir, that he had gone to Mr. Obenreizer's.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: To be sure! His heart is set on that pretty young lady, Sally—he has gone to propose for her. My dear good George! I am well enough still to feel all my old interest in his happiness! Send to Mr. Obenriezer's, Sally —say I want to see them both; Mr. Obenreizer and Mr. Vendale.
George doesn't distrust him as Bintrey does—George will help me.

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: You are not fit to see them, sir.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: I insist on seeing them!

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: If I do send, will you promise to go back to your room, and try to compose yourself?

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Yes! yes! Do it.

sp.speaker: Sally
sp.stage: (opening the door for him to go in).
sp.p: It shall be done, sir.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Thank you! You have relieved my mind.
sp.stage: (Stops and turns round at the door.)
sp.p: You are very little altered, Sally, since the old times. Mr. Obenreizer says the world is so small that the same people are always crossing each other in it again and again. Here are you and I together once more. It seems as if I was coming round again to the Foundling to die.

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: You are not going to die, dear Mr. Wilding!

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.p: Send where I told you.

div.stage: (He goes into the room.)

sp.speaker: Sally
sp.p: It's a risk, I'm afraid, in his state. But I have promised to do it—and I must!

div.stage: (She goes out at the side.)

div.head: Third Scene.
div.stage: —The Cellars at Cripple Corner. Heavy growths of red-tinged fungus hang from the vaulted roof. Casks of all sizes occupy the place. Above and between the casks are deep, dark recesses, used as “bins” for the bottled wine. A ray of daylight streams down through the entrance, which communicates by steps with the court-yard above. Heavy stone pillars support the roof. The darkness, except where the daylight falls, is dimly illuminated, here and there, by a lamp. In some places the obscurity is complete. Joey Ladle is discovered occupied with his measuring rod and his cellar book, measuring spaces, and making entries. He finds his way from one place to another by the help of his cellar lamp. The lamp gives a flickering and uncertain light. While Joey is still absorbed in his work, Vendale appears at the entrance above, descends slowly into the cellar, and advances to the front.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I can't find it in my heart to go into the house. I should vex poor Wilding if I told him what has happened between Obenreizer and me. My own spirits are depressed by the interview, now that the excitement of it is over. Can I do what I said I would do in the heat of the moment? Can I double the value of this business in a year's time? I don't know—I can settle to nothing today. I have been wandering about the streets without aim or object. And here I am, as restless as ever, wandering about the cellars, I don't know why.
Oh! you're here, are you, Joey?

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Oughtn't it rather to go, “Oh! you're here, are you, Master George?” It's my business to be here—but it ain't yourn.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Don't grumble, Joey!

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Oh! I don't grumble. If anything grumbles, it's what I've took in through the pores—it ain't me. Have a care as something in you don't begin a-grumbling, Master George. Stop here long enough for the Wapours to work, and they'll be at it. Yes; they'll be at it—trust 'em.
sp.stage: (Turning away to go on with his work.)
sp.p: And so you've regularly come into the business, Master George?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I hope you don't object, Joey?

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: I don't, bless you! But Wapours objects that you and your partner are both on you too young. You and young Master Wilding have been and changed the name of the firm. If you'd been old enough to know better, you wouldn't have done that. Mark my words! You've changed the luck of the firm—and you'll find it out!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Pooh! nonsense!

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: “Pooh” 's easy said—and “nonsense” follows it naterally enough! I ain't been down here all my life for nothing. I know, by what I notices down here, when it's a-going to rain, when it's a-going to hold up, when it's a-going to blow, when it's a-going to be calm. I know, by what I notices down here, when the luck's changed, quite as well!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.stage: (holding up his lamp to the fungus on the roof).
sp.p: Has this hideous-looking growth anything to do with your divination? We are famous for the fungus in this vault, are we not?

div.stage: (Takes up the measuring rod, and moves the fungus backwards and forwards, slowly.)

sp.speaker: Joey
sp.p: We are, Master George. If you'll be advised by me, you'll let that alone!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Ay, indeed? Why?

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: For three good reasons, Master George.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Let's hear them! First reason, for letting the fungus alone—?

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Because it rises from the casks of wine, and you had better not know what sort of stuff a cellarman takes into himself when he walks in the same all the days of his life.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Second reason?

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Because at a stage of its growth it's maggots— and you might fetch 'em down upon you.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Is it maggots there?

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Not that one, Master George. That one's growed out of the maggots.
I wouldn't keep on touchin' it, sir, if I was you!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Why not?

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: For the third reason, Master George, which I haven't mentioned yet.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Well! what is the third reason?

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Take a look at it's colour first!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I am looking at it.

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Is it like clotted blood?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Like enough, perhaps.

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: More than like enough, I think.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Say it's exactly like. What then?

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Master George! They do say—

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Who?

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: How should I know who? Them as says pretty well everything! How can I give 'em a name, if you can't?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: True. Go on.

div.stage: (A momentary pause. Obenreizer appears in the stream of daylight at the top of the steps. He advances into the cellar, now lost in the darkness, now visible again in the dim lamplight. Neither Vendale nor Joey notice him.)

sp.speaker: Joey
sp.p: They do say, that the man as gets by accident a piece of that dark growth right upon his breast—

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Right upon his breast—

sp.speaker: Joey
sp.p: —will for sure and certain—

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: For sure and certain—

sp.speaker: Joey
sp.p: —die by Murder.
sp.stage: (Suddenly striking Vendale on the breast, with a cry of horror.)
sp.p: By the Lord! you've got a bit of it on you!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: A bit of it on me? Yes! there it is on the ground.

sp.speaker: Joey
sp.stage: (holding up the cellar lamp, and disclosing a large red stain on the front of Vendale's shirt).
sp.p: And there's the mark on your shirt—as red as blood!

div.stage: (Obenreizer suddenly appears before them.)

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: What do you want here?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: I owe you an apology, Mr. Vendale—and I have come here to make it. I don't alter the terms on which I give you my ward in marriage. But I regret the violence of language and manner with which those terms were imposed on you. I ask your pardon.
Will you shake hands with me?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Mr. Obenreizer, I accept your apology!
sp.stage: (Takes his hand, and drops it, shuddering.)
sp.p: Excuse my noticing it—your hand is very cold.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: A heavy heart makes a cold hand, Mr. Vendale. Another errand brings me here, besides my errand of apology. There is sad reason for my saying the words which have made us friends again.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: What is it?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: I have earned the right to offer you my sympathy —and I do offer it. A message came to my house, soon after you had left, summoning us both to Mr. Wilding's presence. I presumed you had gone to him before me—I followed you, as I thought, to the house here. Nothing had been heard of you; and I came to the cellars to inquire for you myself. Mr. Vendale! rouse your courage. I bring miserable news.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Wilding? Let me go to him directly!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Wait! He has had a second fit.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Dead?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Dead!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Oh, my poor Walter! My dear, dear friend!
sp.stage: (A pause. Vendale turns to Joey, and points to the stain on the front of his shirt.)
sp.p: You said this was a warning of death. How little we thought that your superstition would come true!

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: I said more than that, Master George! Death was not the word.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: What was the word?

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Murder.

div.head: First Scene.
div.stage: —The Counting-house at Cripple Corner. A door at the side. A door in the flat scene, opening on the court-yard of the First Act. Vendale and Sally Goldstraw discovered. They are both dressed in mourning.

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Have you any more orders to give me, sir?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: No.—Stop! I have a question to ask you. Now that poor Wilding is buried, many things occur to me, which it was impossible to think of when we first felt the calamity of his death. How came Mr. Obenreizer to be present at his last moments?

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Mr. Wilding insisted, sir, on sending for Mr. Obenreizer—I don't know why.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: It seems strange, certainly! What could there be in common between them? On the first day of Mr. Obenreizer's arrival in England, I remember poor Wilding looking at him with an appearance of extraordinary interest, and speaking to Mr. Bintrey in a very earnest way. My attention was occupied at the time; and I paid no heed to what passed between them.—Tell me exactly what happened, Sally, on the day of Mr. Wilding's death.

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: I sent for Mr. Obenreizer, sir, and I sent for you —I did it to pacify my poor master. The messenger found Mr. Obenreizer at home; but nobody knew where to find you.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I had bad news to tell my poor friend; and I purposely kept out of the way of telling it.—Go on.

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Mr. Wilding got more and more disturbed in his mind, sir, while the messenger was gone. I sent for the doctor; and the doctor persuaded him to get to bed. But there was no quieting him that way. He insisted on knowing it, when Mr. Obenreizer came alone to the house. He declared he would leave his bed, and go down-stairs— unless Mr. Obenreizer was brought up to see him. The doctor said to me, “The risk of irritating him, in his present state, is the worst risk of all. Let the person come up.”

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Well?

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: The moment Mr. Obenreizer came into the room, sir, my poor master started up in his bed, and looked at his visitor with a dreadful eagerness, and fought and struggled for breath to speak. The doctor ordered Mr. Obenreizer out of the room again instantly. It was too late. The only sound that passed Mr. Wilding's lips was the sound of your name, sir. The fit took him the moment after, and it was all over. He spoke in a thick, husky way—but I am sure he spoke your name.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I don't doubt it, Sally. I am charged by his will to accomplish the one object which we all know he had at heart—the finding of the lost namesake, whose place he had innocently usurped. The uppermost thought in his mind, when he felt death coming, was to rely on me. My poor dead friend—I will be true to your trust! If the lost man lives, you shall not have reckoned on my help in vain!
sp.stage: (A knock is heard at the door leading into the yard.)
sp.p: Who's there?

div.stage: (Joey Ladle opens the door. He carries a letter in his hand.)

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Me, sir.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Wait one moment.
sp.stage: (Joey waits at the door. Vendale turns to Sally.)
sp.p: One last question. Did Mr. Obenreizer make any remark, when he was first told of Wilding's death?

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: He only said, sir, that he was shocked to hear of it; and that he would go and break the news to you.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: The mystery of what Wilding wanted with him remains as impenetrable as ever. Perhaps time may clear it up, Sally!
Well—what is it?

sp.speaker: Joey
sp.p: A letter, sir, from foreign parts.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: From our correspondents in Switzerland! From Defresnier and Company, the wine-merchants of Neuchâtel!

div.stage: (Opens and reads the letter.)

sp.speaker: Joey
sp.p: Do you find yourself a little easier, Miss, now they've put poor Master Wilding in the ground? There's no consolation going, like the consolation of a funeral—provided the undertaker does his duty.

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: We must all learn to submit to our losses in this world, Mr. Joey. I am learning, I hope, to submit to mine.

div.stage: (She goes out by the side door.)

sp.speaker: Joey
sp.p: Beautiful language! The parson himself couldn't have put it prettier than that!
I'll say it over again, after her, like the catechism. “We must all submit to learning, Mr. Joey—which is one of our losses in this world.” Lord! how true!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Another misfortune, coming close on Wilding's death! A loss of five hundred pounds, at the time of all others when money is of most consequence to me!

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Anything wrong, Master Vendale?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: As wrong as can be, Joey.

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Ah! I said it would come. “You've been and changed the name of the firm; mind you haven't been and changed the luck of the firm!” My own words to him as is gone. It's foreign to my nature, Master George, to crow over the house I serve. Please to understand, I don't set myself up for a prophet!
You won't get over it, that way, sir! You'd better open your heart to me. I know what's at the bottom of this—it's them six cases of red wine.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: The devil take the six cases of red wine!

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: The devil brought 'em, sir!
sp.stage: (Vendale withdraws to an office-desk, smoothes out the letter, takes other letters from the desk, and compares them one with the other. Joey goes on.)
sp.p: Now let's put the thing plainly. Here's a large consignment of Swiss champagne comes to this house, from our foreign correspondents at the place they call Nooshattle. And among that consignment I find six cases of red wine that didn't ought to be. I says to myself, “In the time of Pebbleson Nephew no mistake was ever made in a consignment delivered at these doors; the luck's gone—Lord help us at Cripple Corner! the luck's gone!” And what follows? You write out, sir, to tell 'em at Nooshattle of the mistake. And they write back to you. Not satisfied on your side, you write again. Not satisfied on their side, they write again. There's their letter on the desk before you, as full of bad news as an egg's full of meat! And here am I that foretold it all—took it in, you may say, at the pores. Do I crow over the house I serve? No! Do I set myself up for a prophet? No! I return, with molloncolly steps, to the Wapours below—respectfully reminding you, sir, of what that precious woman, Miss Goldstraw, said just now. “We must all submit to losses, Mr. Joey—which is one of our learnings in this world.” Golden words, Master George. Take 'em to heart, sir! take 'em to heart!

div.stage: (Exit into the yard.)

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Letter number one:—I write to tell Defresnier and Company of the red wine being sent with the white. And I refer incidentally to a payment of five hundred pounds made by our house to theirs, some time since. Letter number two:—Defresniers write back to apologise for the mistake, and then add that the five hundred pounds alluded to has never been received by their house. Letter number three:—I write back, enclosing them a copy of their own receipt for the sum. Letter number four—is Defresniers' answer, just put into my hands.
sp.stage: (Leaving the desk, and coming forward with the letter in his hand.)
sp.p: Let me read it again.

“Dear Sir,—I write to you, in the absence of my partner who has gone on business to Milan. The receipt of which you enclose a copy can be nothing but a forgery. The remittance of five hundred pounds must have been intercepted and stolen on its way to our hands. Suspicion points at a person who was not long since in our employment.
