We refrain from mentioning his name, until we are sure of his guilt.”—Who can this man be? In my position, it is useless to inquire!—“Let us at once see the original receipt, and compare the handwriting in it, with certain specimens of handwriting in our possession. Don't trust the post. Send a private messenger—and let him be a man who has been long in your service; who is accustomed to travelling, who is capable of speaking French, and who can be trusted to let no stranger scrape acquaintance with him on the route.”—Where am I to find the man, in this office? None of the clerks are accustomed to travelling abroad. None of the clerks can speak French. And what is the reason for this extraordinary caution? Here it is:—“If the person whom we suspect is really guilty, circumstances may have occurred to put him on his guard—and, in that case, he is a man to hesitate at nothing, if he can get possession of the receipt which is the only evidence against him. Tell no one in existence of the turn things have taken. Everything depends on your interpreting literally the warning I give you in this letter.”—I know the man who writes those words—I am certain he would not have written them, without a serious reason for it. What am I to do? I have nobody whom I can rely on to send.

div.stage: (Obenreizer enters from the court-yard, shown in by Joey. Joey stands apart for a moment, watching.)

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: A thousand pardons! I am afraid I disturb you!

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: It was him as stole in when that bit of stuff fell on Master George's breast! It's him as steals in again, now, when bad news comes to Master George. He brings ill luck. I don't like Mr. Openrazor!

div.stage: (Joey returns to the yard, looking back suspiciously, before he closes the door.)

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Is there any business this morning that I can do?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: You come at a bad time, Mr. Obenreizer. You find my business threatened with a loss of five hundred pounds.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Five hundred pounds!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: A remittance of ours to that amount has been stolen from the correspondents to whom we sent it.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Stolen!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: And a forged receipt sent to us in their name— the name of your old employers, Defresnier and Company.

div.stage: (He looks again at the letter in his hand.)

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: How—how has it happened?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: There is the correspondence. You can see for yourself.
sp.stage: (Obenreizer goes to the desk, and reads the letters. Vendale continues, aside.)
sp.p: Obenreizer was in Defresnier's employment. He may be able to throw some light upon it! Suppose I show him the forged receipt?
sp.stage: (Takes a key and opens the door of the iron safe in which his papers are kept.)

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Has he got the receipt? Oh, if he only takes it out of the safe!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Here it is!
sp.stage: (He drops the letter which he has hitherto kept mechanically in his hand— picks it up again—and looks at it. At the same moment Obenreizer stealthily advances a step towards him from the desk—then looks back to see that the door leading into the yard is closed. Vendale continues.)
sp.p: The letter! I had forgotten the caution. I am warned to trust nobody.

div.stage: (He returns to the safe, and stands before it, hesitating, with his back towards Obenreizer.)

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Not a soul to see us! And I am the strongest of the two!

div.stage: (At the moment when he is within arm's length of Vendale, the door from the court-yard is loudly opened, and Joey reappears. Obenreizer starts back.)

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Did you call, Master George?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: No! Don't interrupt us!

sp.speaker: Joey
sp.stage: (aside, after a suspicious look at Obenreizer).
sp.p: I won't shut the door this time!

div.stage: (He goes out, leaving the door into the yard open.)

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Well? Have you read the letters?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: I can't tell you how surprised and sorry I am! Let us hope there is some mistake.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I have another letter, received this morning, which confirms the news.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: May I see it?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: It forbids me to act on my own discretion; otherwise you should see it directly.

div.stage: (He turns to lock the safe. At the same moment Obenreizer turns, and looks towards the yard. The door is wide open, and Joey and his men are passing backwards and forwards within view.)

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Force is hopeless. I'll try fraud!
Suppose you show me the receipt?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: The very thing I was thinking of! But there's an obstacle in the way. This letter insists on my keeping the whole thing a profound secret from everybody.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Without excepting me? Surely they must have forgotten—?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: No doubt they have forgotten! I had thought of asking your advice. And more—the receipt must be conveyed to Switzerland by private hand. I don't know who I can trust—

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Take it yourself—and I'll go with you. Nothing could happen better. I came to tell you this morning that I have business which forces me to go to Switzerland.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Leave Marguerite!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: If Defresnier's partner had remembered what he ought to have remembered, he would have saved you a world of trouble. As it is, what can you do? You are acting in a very serious matter, and acting entirely in the dark. As a man of business, you have no choice. You must be guided, not by the spirit, but by the letter of your instructions. You must go as I go—at once!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I must speak to Marguerite first.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: By all means! Come and dine at my house— bring your luggage with you—and we will start by the mail train together. Is it agreed?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Agreed!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: At seven to-night?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: At seven to-night.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: You take the receipt of course?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I take the receipt.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: And I take it from you on the road!

div.stage: (Exit.)

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: I'll carry your luggage, sir, to Mr. Openrazor's house.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: You have been listening!

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Not exactly, sir; but I've heard everything, for all that!

div.stage: (The Scene closes.)

div.head: Second Scene.
div.stage: —A room in Wilding's house—the room already shown in the Second Scene of the Second Act. Enter Sally Goldstraw, followed by Joey.

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Mr. Joey!

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Miss Goldstraw!

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Your proper place is in the cellars; and my proper place is in the house.

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: If you prefer the cellars, Miss, I'll follow you, there, with the greatest pleasure.

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Why do you want to follow me at all?

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: For the reason, Miss, that the first man followed the first woman—because he took a liking to her!

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: And the first woman, Mr. Joey, led him all wrong afterwards. I don't desire to lead you wrong. I wish you good morning.

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Please to stop where you are, Miss. There's another reason for my follering you. I'm uneasy in my mind.

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: How can I help that?

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: How can you help that? I'll tell you. What do you do, when you cut your finger, and it hurts you? You take a bit of rag, and you smear a bit of balsam on it, and you clap the whole on the place, and you're all right again. I'm the cut finger; and you're the balsam and the rag.

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: I'm much obliged to you, Mr. Joey, for likening me to balsam and rag!

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: You're heartily welcome, Miss! At the same time, if you please, we won't lose sight of the state of my mind. P'r'aps it's the Wapours I've took in at the pores. P'r'aps it's the gift of prophesying which has come strong on me lately? Whether it's one, or whether it's t'other, I'm uneasy in my mind about the way things is going on in this house. Now just look into the matter, to please me!
sp.stage: (Attempts to put his arm round her waist.)

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: I don't look at things with my waist, Mr. Joey— and you don't look at things with your arm!
sp.stage: (Aside, after a glance at Joey's leather apron.)
sp.p: How can a man possibly fall in love, when he wears such an apron as that?

sp.speaker: Joey
sp.p: She likes my apron. What follers her liking my apron? She likes me!

Look at it, Miss, with any part of you you please, so long as you do look at it. It all begun with poor Master Wilding changing the name of the Firm. He changed the luck of the Firm, when he did that. What happens afterwards? He dies to begin with. Then, a bit of that cursed stuff in the cellars falls on Master George. Then, a letter comes from foreign parts, and brings bad news. And now, here's Master George going away from us in a hurry, in company with that Mr. Openrazor, who turns my stomach whenever I look at him. If something ain't done to bring the luck round, you mark my words—it will end badly!

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Bring the luck round! Why are you looking at me? Who's to do it?

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: You!

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: I! What can you be thinking of? Why, I am the cause—the innocent cause, Mr. Joey—of everything that you complain of! If I had not come here to apply for the situation, poor Mr. Wilding need never have known the truth—and all the rest of it need never have happened. If you know your own mind, you ought to hate me! I am the miserable creature who has brought the ill luck into the house—

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: All the more reason, Miss, for you to bring the good luck back again.
That was well said, I think!

sp.speaker: Sally
sp.p: He has evidently fallen in love with me, in spite of his apron!

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: You can do it, Miss, as easy as one and one make two.

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: How, Mr. Joey?

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: By changing your name, Miss, from Goldstraw (which is good) to Ladle (which is better).
That was well said, I think!

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: What, Mr. Joey! You, of all the people in the world, recommend me to change the name of the Firm? What next, I wonder?

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: A woman's not a Firm, Miss. And Lord forbid she ever should be!

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: The women are much obliged to you, Mr. Joey, for another compliment!

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: The women are heartily welcome, Miss Goldstraw.

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: You have a very sudden way of making love. Have you ever done it before?

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: I've tried, Miss—but I never got as far as this. I would be slower about it, I do assure you, if I only had the time. The Wapours are waiting for me. And, after the Wapours, there Master George's luggage to be taken to Mr. Openrazor's house. And, after that, there's no knowing, in the state of my mind, what may happen next. I think I might persuade you, Miss, if I might make so bold as to speak with my arm—and if you'd be so obliging as to listen with your waist.

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: The “Wapours” are not waiting for me, Mr. Joey; and I want time to decide.
The institution of marriage is a very serious thing. And the sooner a man and a woman learn to view it in that light, the better it may be afterwards for all parties.—I wish you good morning!

div.stage: (Exit, right.)

sp.speaker: Joey
sp.p: Beautiful language! I'll fix it in my mind, before I forget it.
“The institution of a man and a woman is a very serious thing. And the sooner they're married afterwards, the better for all parties.” Lord! how true!

div.stage: (Exit, left.)

div.head: Third Scene.
div.stage: —The drawing-room at Obenreizer's lodgings —as shown in the First Scene of the Second Act: with this difference, that it is now supposed to be night, and the lamps are lit. Dinner, untouched, is on the table. Marguerite, Obenreizer, and Vendale are discovered. The two last wear their travelling costume. Obenreizer is on his knees, at the back of the stage, packing a portmanteau. Vendale, near the front, sits thoughtfully at the table, with a cigar in his mouth, which he has allowed to go out. His luggage, ready for the journey, is seen in a corner of the room. Marguerite, restless and agitated, passes backwards and forwards, giving Obenreizer the various things he wants to pack for the journey. These different objects are so arranged on a side table, as to oblige Marguerite to pass and repass Vendale on her way backwards and forwards. The words she says to Vendale, at the beginning of the scene, are all spoken in an under tone of warning at the time when she passes him. Madame Dor sits in an unoccupied part of the stage, with her back turned as usual, cleaning the gloves with which Obenreizer is going to travel.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: I really can't allow you, dearest, to wait upon me in this way! You must not fatigue yourself by going backwards and forwards with my things for the journey!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: I am not in the least fatigued—and I beg to be allowed to help you.
sp.stage: (She returns to the side table, takes up the next thing wanted, and, stopping a moment, speaks to Vendale, on her way back to Obenreizer.)
sp.p: Change your mind, George! Don't travel with him!

div.stage: (She goes on to Obenreizer.)

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: How strangely she persists in warning me not to go! The suddenness of this journey has shaken her nerves.
There is really nothing, love, to alarm you!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.stage: (passing back by Vendale, from the side table).
sp.p: You know the little photograph I have got of you. This afternoon he took it up, and looked at it.
sp.stage: (Goes on to Obenreizer—returns—and continues to Vendale.)
sp.p: I saw his face in the glass when he looked at your portrait. George! you have offended him!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: He is as merciless as a tiger! He is as secret as the grave! Don't go with him, George!

div.stage: (Goes on with the next travelling article to Obenreizer.)

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: My darling! you are completely mistaken.
sp.stage: (Marguerite takes the next thing from the table, without answering. Vendale continues as she passes back.)
sp.p: He and I were never better friends than we are at this moment!

div.stage: (Marguerite shakes her head, and goes on to Obenreizer.)

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Don't go, George!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I know, love, how hard it is to part—!
sp.stage: (Marguerite disengages herself, and fetches the last thing from the table.)

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: I can submit to the parting, if you will only go alone!
sp.stage: (Passes on to Obenreizer, and comes back rapidly to Vendale, before Obenreizer can close his portmanteau.)
sp.p: It will be too late in a minute more! Change your mind, George! change your mind!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Ten thousand thanks, Marguerite, for your help! Vendale! Time gallops with us travellers—in five minutes more, we must be off!
sp.stage: (Vendale rises, and tries to quiet Marguerite, while Obenreizer is looking for his courier's bag.)
sp.p: My travelling-bag?—Ah! here it is!
sp.stage: (He takes the bag from a chair, opens it, and addresses Vendale.)
sp.p: Can I take anything for you? You have no travelling-bag. Here is the compartment for papers, open at your service!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Many thanks. I have only one paper of importance about me, and that paper I am bound to take charge of myself. I won't part with it till we get to Neuchâtel.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Won't you!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Look at him now!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Madame Dor! my gloves!
sp.stage: (Madame Dor hands them to him over her shoulder.)
sp.p: Guardian angel of my baggage—beautifully cleaned!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: You hear him? He is in the best possible spirits! You are frightened, darling, at your own fancy.

div.stage: Enter Joey Ladle.

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Master George!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: The luggage is all right, Joey! You needn't wait.

sp.speaker: Joey
sp.p: I've brought you another letter, sir, from foreign parts. It's been sent on, by private express, from Dover to our office.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Is your journey put off?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: News from the Swiss Firm?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Let me read the letter!
sp.stage: (Marguerite, Obenreizer, and Joey all draw aside, and all eagerly watch Vendale. Vendale reads the letter.)
sp.p: “Sir, —Not half an hour after our second partner, Monsieur Rolland, had written to you, a deplorable calamity happened in his family. A fatal accident has deprived him of his son and only child. Monsieur Rolland, overwhelmed by this misfortune, is unable to attend to any business, and has been ordered away by his medical man. Our other partner—Monsieur Defresnier—is, as you know, detained at Milan by business. In this condition of things, I am obliged to request you to send the forged receipt on to M. Defresnier who is alone competent to deal with the question, in the present affliction of the other principal of our Firm. I have sent the necessary office-papers to Milan. And I entreat you, in your own interests, as well as in ours, to lose no time. Your obedient servant, (chief clerk in the house of Defresnier and Company).”

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Well?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Well?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I am afraid you will be disappointed. The journey is lengthened—we must go to Milan.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: My last hope gone!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: I breathe again!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: There is no objection to your seeing this letter. There is even a reason for your seeing it. You have engaged to accompany me as far as Switzerland. In this winter weather, I can scarcely expect you to go on with me, and cross the Alps.

div.stage: (Hands the letter to Obenreizer.)

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: My friend! I do nothing by halves. If you cross the Alps—winter or summer, I cross them with you!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Bravely said, brother-traveller! Joey! take a pen, and alter the address on my portmanteau from Neuchâtel to Milan. Do you know how to spell it? MILAN.
sp.stage: (He speaks aside with Marguerite, trying to compose her. Obenreizer silently reads the letter.)

sp.speaker: Joey
sp.p: I can spell out more than that, Master George! I can spell out that Miss Margaret don't like this journey of yours no better than I do. I'd give something to hear what she has to say about it.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Witnesses may intrude themselves on the railways. Servants may be in the way at the inns. On the mountain, there are neither witnesses nor servants! On the mountain, I have got him!
En route, my friend! We have not another minute to spare.

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: I'll take your luggage, Master George. The cab's at the door.
sp.stage: (Takes out Vendale's luggage. Madame Dor follows in triumph with Obenreizer's portmanteau.)

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Adieu, my charming ward! Remember me in my absence, Marguerite, as kindly as you can. I know how precious he is to you. Trust to me—I'll take care of him!

div.stage: (Exit.)

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Oh, George! don't, don't, don't go!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Vendale!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Compose yourself, my angel! In less than a month, I shall be back again!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Vendale!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: One last kiss!

div.stage: Joey re-enters.

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: He's a-waiting for you, Master George.

div.stage: (Vendale hurries out.)

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Gone! Gone in spite of all I could say to him! What's to be done?

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Give me your hand, Miss—and I'll tell you!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Both! both!

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Look at me!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: I do! I do!

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Have you got courage enough to do a desperate thing?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Try me! I'm no fine lady. I'm one of the people, Joey, like you!

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: It's borne in on your mind that he's in danger; and it's borne in on mine.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Yes!

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: He has gone, past all calling back.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Yes! yes!

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Follow him, Miss. And I'll go with you!

div.stage: (Marguerite clasps her hands with a cry of delight. The curtain falls.)

div.head: First Scene.
div.stage: —A bedroom in a Swiss inn. Time, night. The bed is at the back of the stage. At the side, a door. A small table near the door. A heavy latch on the inner side of the door. At the opposite side, a fireplace. The candles on the table are burning low in their sockets. The red light of the fire is the principal light in the room. Vendale is discovered, lying on a sofa. Obenreizer is with him, walking backwards and forwards in the room.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: How still the night is! I hear a rushing sound somewhere in the distance. Is it a waterfall?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Yes. A waterfall on the lower slopes of the mountain.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: The mountain that lies between us and Italy! The mountain that we cross to-morrow!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.stage: (stopping in his walk, and pursuing his own train of thought).
sp.p: It sounds like the old waterfall at home. The waterfall which my mother showed to travellers—if she was my mother!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: If she was your mother?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: The sound of that waterfall changed with the weather, as does the sound of all falling waters, and flowing waters. I remember it as sometimes saying to me for whole days—“Who are you, my little wretch?—Who are you, my little wretch?”—I remember it other times saying, when its sound was hollow, and storm was coming up the pass—“Boom! Boom! Boom! Beat him! Beat him! Beat him!” like my mother in a rage—if she was my mother.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Why do you say “if”?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: What do I know about it? I am so obscurely born, how can I say? I was young: the rest of my family were men and women. My so-called parents were old. Anything is possible of a case like mine.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Did you ever doubt—?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Bah! Here I am in the world. What does it matter how I come there?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: At least you are Swiss?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: How do I know? I say to you: “At least you are English.” How do you know?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: By what I have been told from infancy.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: You believe what you have been told from infancy? Good! To cut it short—I will believe what I have been told from infancy, too.

div.stage: (Resumes his walk up and down the room.)

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Have you no recollections of your early days?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: I have recollections of feeling hunger; I have recollections of feeling cold; I have recollections of feeling the stick! There is the biography of my early days! Pity me or laugh at me, which you please—and then forget all about me, as soon as possible. Twenty years ago I should have begged your loose halfpence of you. Now, all I beg of you is—to change the subject!

div.stage: (Goes to the window, opens the shutter, and looks out.)

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: There is something he won't confess about his early life. Is there any clue here to what Wilding wanted with him in the bygone time?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Dark and cold, my brother-traveller! Not a creature passing on the earth! Not a star to be seen in the heaven! Your fire is burning low—we must mend it.
sp.stage: (Goes to the door and calls off.)
sp.p: More wood!
sp.stage: (The Waiter enters, and puts wood on the fire. Obenreizer continues; standing near the door, and speaking to himself.)
sp.p: Where will he put the receipt to-night? If he sleeps, I shall find out. But suppose he wakes? I'll make sure.
I'll try the laudanum tonight.

sp.speaker: The Waiter
sp.p: Any more orders, sir.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: No more orders.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Yes! one more order! Bring some of the best brandy you have in the house.
The cold is piercing, in spite of all the fire we can make here. A little brandy will do neither of us any harm.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I am afraid it will be bad brandy in such a place as this.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Our flasks are empty—bad brandy is better than none.
sp.stage: (The Waiter enters with brandy and two wine-glasses on a tray.)
sp.p: Put it here.

div.stage: (The Waiter puts the tray on the table near the door.)

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Have you got your orders for the morning?
sp.stage: (The Waiter crosses to Vendale. Obenreizer, with his back towards them, drugs a glass of brandy at the table. Vendale continues to the Waiter.)
sp.p: Do the guides know that we want them for crossing the mountain?

sp.speaker: The Waiter.
sp.p: Yes, sir.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: You are to call us early, mind.

sp.speaker: The Waiter.
sp.p: At four o'clock, sir?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: At four o'clock.
sp.stage: (The Waiter goes out. Obenreizer crosses with the drugged brandy to Vendale.)

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: You are a judge of these things. Try it, and tell me.
Bad, I'm afraid?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: It has a coarse after-flavour. I don't like it!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: There is a little still left in the glass. I'll try it next.
Booh! It burns! Vile bad brandy; as you say!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: The time is getting on, isn't it? Look at your watch; mine has stopped.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: The time is getting on! We must get what rest we can. One word before I leave you. When you are travelling, do you lock your door at night?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Not I! I sleep too soundly.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: You sleep so soundly? What a blessing!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Anything but a blessing to the rest of the house, if they had to knock me up from the outside of the door! If the waiter comes in and wakes me, I shall not disturb the other people in the inn.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: I understand. I leave my room open also. But let me advise you one thing. I am a Swiss who knows. When you travel in my country, always put your papers— and your money also, of course—under your pillow. Always under your pillow!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: You are not complimentary to your countrymen!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: My countrymen are like the majority of men. The majority of men will take what they can get. Adieu! At four in the morning.

div.stage: (Exit.)

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.stage: (rising from the sofa and mending the fire).
sp.p: My travelling-companion is a strange fellow. And the strangest part of him is—what he said just now about his early life. I fancy I can guess, for the first time, what poor Wilding wanted with him. It seems wonderful now that the thing never struck me before. The adopted child was taken to Switzerland, as we know. Obenreizer is Wilding's age. Obenreizer doubts if his parents were his parents. Obenreizer speaks English with so little accent, that English might have been the first language he learnt. Is the lost man now sleeping in the next room to me?
My head feels heavy—the effect of the cold, I suppose?
sp.stage: (Puts more wood on the fire, and crouches over it, warming himself.)
sp.p: Poor Wilding's last wishes are sacred to me. His whole fortune is left to the missing man—and that man is not found yet. I'll question Obenreizer more closely!
My head feels heavier and heavier. That bad brandy is affecting me already, no doubt. Foolish of me to drink even the little I did.
sp.stage: (Stops, pursuing the former train of thought.)
sp.p: Suppose it turns out that Obenreizer is the missing man? Should I like him to be the real Wilding? I get on very well with him, but I should hardly like that. Should I like him to be rich? No—he has influence enough over Marguerite as it is, and wealth might give him more.
sp.stage: (A pause, his head sinks on his breast—he rouses himself by an effort.)
sp.p: What am I thinking of? Ought any likings or dislikings of mine to stand between me and the discharge of my duty to my dead friend? No! Come what may of it, that duty shall be done. To-morrow —when my head is clearer—I'll think of it again.
sp.stage: (Goes to the window and looks out, closes the shutter, and returns to the sofa.)
sp.p: I'm in bad condition for crossing the mountain. My legs feel weary, only with walking about the room.
An hour's rest will put me right—the sofa is nearest the fire. I feel sleep coming on me—I'll stop here.
sp.stage: (Closes his eyes. For a few moments nothing happens on the stage; then the candles go out suddenly in their sockets. The firelight is left in the room. In a moment more the heavy latch on the inner side of the door is raised softly. The door opens by an inch at a time, and Obenreizer steals in. He wears nothing but his trousers and his flannel shirt. The collar of the shirt is thrown open, and the sleeves are turned up to the elbows. Advancing towards the bed, his foot strikes against the table. Vendale starts up and rushes across the stage to him.)

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: What now? Who is it?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.stage: (surprised and seizing him by the shoulders).
sp.p: Not in bed yet! Then something is wrong!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: What do you mean?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: First tell me—are you ill?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Ill? No.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: I have had a bad dream about you. I tried to rest after it, but it was impossible. I was anxious to know you were safe—and yet I was afraid you would laugh at me! I have been minutes hesitating at the door—I have at last come in. You satisfy me that my dream was a dream—shall I leave you again? My fire has gone the way of your candles. Do you wish to sleep?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I was sleepy enough before you came in. The surprise seems to have roused me. Stop here, and keep me company—and welcome.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Ah! it was a bad dream! I thought you were ill—I thought I had a wrestle with a robber. You see I was stripped for it?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.stage: (pointing to a dagger in the belt round Obenreizer's waist).
sp.p: And armed too, I see?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: A traveller's dagger that I always carry on the road. Do you carry no such thing?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Nothing of the kind.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.stage: (moving towards the bed and looking at the pillow).
sp.p: And no pistols?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: No arms of any sort.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: You Englishmen are so confident!
sp.stage: (Feels under the pillow, and continues aside.)
sp.p: The receipt is not there. Has he got it about him?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Where are you?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: I am here.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I had something I wanted to ask you. I intended to ask it to-morrow. Why not now?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Why not, if you can remember it?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: It was something very important. You were concerned in it—You know what it is—

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Something about to-morrow?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Yes—to-morrow.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: The laudanum has done its work at last! Now to find the receipt! It is not under his pillow! Has he by any chance forgotten, and put it in his valise?
No! not there. Has he been looking at it, and left it anywhere about the room?
sp.stage: (Lights a match, and looks about the room.)
sp.p: No! It is not left about the room. It must be on him—he said in London he would keep it about him. Have I given the laudanum time enough? Yes!

There he lies helpless at my mercy—the man who has come between me and Marguerite—the man who carries my ruin in the pocket of his coat—the man whose life I doubly thirst to take! Patience! patience! The inn is lonely; but the mountain is lonelier still!
sp.stage: (Feels over the breast-pocket of Vendale's coat.)
sp.p: Has he got it here? Softly! Softly! Let me unbutton his coat.
sp.stage: (As he unbuttons Vendale's coat, a loud knock is heard at the door of the room.)

sp.speaker: The Waiter
sp.p: Four o'clock, gentlemen!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Who's there? Come in!
sp.stage: (The Waiter enters the room, Obenreizer crosses to the door as the Waiter crosses to Vendale.)

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: He crosses the mountain with me to-day. On the mountain I'll kill him!

div.stage: (The Scene closes on them.)

div.head: Second Scene.
div.stage: —The exterior of the Swiss Inn. The day is breaking. The objects of the scene, and the persons of the scene, are only visible as shadows in a mist. Two high peaks of mountains, white with snow, are faintly discernible through the darkness. The Waiter at the inn, and three guides—Jean-Paul, Jean-Baptiste, and Jean-Marie—appear like shadowy figures before the inn door.

sp.speaker: The Waiter.
sp.p: Well, my lads, the day has broken at last. What do you say to the weather, now?

sp.speaker: Jean-Paul.
sp.p: I say the weather will do.

sp.speaker: Jean-Baptiste.
sp.p: I say doubtful!

sp.speaker: Jean-Marie.
sp.p: I say—bad!

sp.speaker: The Waiter.
sp.p: You must make up your minds. The two gentlemen have waited till they can wait no longer.

sp.speaker: Jean-Paul.
sp.p: I am ready to cross the mountain with the gentlemen—if the others will go with me.

sp.speaker: Jean-Baptiste.
sp.p: I should like to consult my father. My father knows the mountain by heart.

sp.speaker: Jean-Marie.
sp.p: I can see for myself that there's a storm coming. I smell the snow, I feel the hurricane, in the air. No money that the gentlemen can offer will tempt me to cross the mountain with them to-day.

div.stage: Enter Obenreizer and Vendale, equipped for crossing the mountain. They are followed by Baptiste Senior.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Well? Are you ready at last?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: My patience is at an end! I am sick and weary of all this doubt and delay!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: You hear what my friend says? Do you cross the mountain with us, or not?

sp.speaker: Jean-Paul.
sp.p: I say yes—if the others will say yes too.

sp.speaker: Jean-Marie.
sp.p: I say, No! Offer me what you like—No!

sp.speaker: Jean-Baptiste.
sp.p: I say—put the case to my father here, and let him settle it. My father, gentlemen, is the oldest guide in these parts. He knows the mountain; he knows the weather; and he speaks the truth.

sp.speaker: The Waiter.
sp.p: You may depend on the old man, gentlemen. I can certify to that!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: You have been in Switzerland before? You know the meaning of this? They want us to double our terms—that's all!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Do they think we are children? Are they attempting to frighten us?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: You shall judge for yourself!
Now, you wise man of the mountains! What weather shall we have to-day?

sp.speaker: Baptiste Senior.
sp.p: You will have a storm to-day.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: What did I tell you?

sp.speaker: Baptiste Senior.
sp.p: You will have snow enough to bury you as you stand upright. You will have wind enough to blow the breath out of your body, and the hair off your head. You will have thunder and lightning. You will feel a cold you never felt before. You will see a darkness you never saw before. If you're weary of your lives, cross the mountain to-day.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Upon my word! a pretty confident opinion.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Bah! Two napoleons would change his opinion.

sp.speaker: Baptiste Senior.
sp.p: Two thousand napoleons wouldn't change it!
Come here, if you please! You haven't said I'm to be bribed—I'll tell you.
Look up there! How many peaks can you count showing white through the mist?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Two.

sp.speaker: Baptiste Senior.
sp.p: There's a third peak.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Why don't I see it?

sp.speaker: Baptiste Senior.
sp.p: Because the storm-cloud is on it already. When that peak is hidden, while the other peaks show—beware of the mountain; there's mischief coming! Did you hear the waterfall last night? Storm! Have you seen the cows restless, and the goats out of temper? Storm! Did your door stick in the jambs when you opened it this morning? Storm! Take your own way. I have warned you—and I wash my hands of it.

sp.speaker: Jean-Baptiste.
sp.p: I say what my father says.

sp.speaker: Jean-Marie.
sp.p: I said as much for myself, before your father spoke.

sp.speaker: Jean-Paul.
sp.p: I can't go, unless the others go too.

sp.speaker: The Waiter.
sp.p: We will do our best, gentlemen, to make you comfortable at the inn.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: A formidable chorus, truly! Decide for yourself, Vendale. Your immortal Shakespeare says somewhere that discretion is the better part of valour.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Fair weather or foul, I have no time to lose—and I am for pushing on.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Don't let me influence you. I am mountain born —I know the pass up there as I know my A B C.— I have heard these poor devils of guides ply their trade in this way, hundreds of times. It's different with you—you may feel inclined to believe them. I'll wait here if you like?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I have waited too long already. I have pressing occasion to cross—

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: You hear? He has pressing occasion to cross.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: You know the mountain. If you will risk it, I will!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: I risk it, at my friend's request.
I'm your man! I'll guide you to your journey's end! Say when—and I am ready!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Now!

sp.speaker: Baptiste Senior
sp.p: One last warning, sir! You didn't tell me I was to be bribed. There are five places of shelter on the road. Past the five places, there is the wooden cross, and there is the convent. When the storm comes on, don't try to brave it. If there is shelter near, take shelter instantly!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: How they stick to their trade! Our old friend here is inimitable. He hasn't given up the hope of plundering you yet!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Are you ready?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Come along!

div.stage: (They go out. Great excitement among the Guides, who follow a few steps, and remain at the side, looking after the travellers eagerly.)

sp.speaker: Jean-Paul
sp.p: Not too fast, gentlemen! Spare your strength at starting!

sp.speaker: Jean-Baptiste
sp.p: Don't forget the shelter on the road!

sp.speaker: Jean-Marie
sp.p: Don't rush on your own destruction. Come back!

sp.speaker: The Waiter
sp.p: When the snow falls, sound the way with your sticks. Keep the Track!

sp.speaker: Baptiste Senior.
sp.p: Spare your breath! They have as much chance of keeping the Track—as you have of being master of this inn.

sp.speaker: The Waiter.
sp.p: I don't know that. They are both stout walkers.

sp.speaker: Baptiste Senior.
sp.p: They are both dead men!

div.stage: (He leads the way into the inn. The others follow. The Scene changes.)

div.head: Third Scene.
div.stage: —The Pass on the Mountain. On the right of the stage, at the back, a steep path winds downward through rock and snow. The path is supposed to lead down from the convent—which is not shown in the Scene —and to connect it with the Track over the mountain. The Track itself crosses the stage longitudinally, from the bottom of the convent path, and is continued, sloping downwards, until it is lost to view off the stage on the left. Along its farther side from the audience, the ground composing the Track rises to a sharp edge, which represents the brink of an unseen precipice. Opposite the Track, and beyond it, the mountain rises again on the other side of the abyss, in steep walls of rock, snow, and ice, and is lost to view at the top of the stage. There is supposed to be a lull in the storm. The snow still falls. But the howling of the wind is low, the lightning comes at long intervals, and the rolling of the thunder in prolonged echoes is only heard faintly in the distance. The wind and the thunder—both low—must continue through the Scene, the voices of the actors being heard above it. On the Scene being disclosed, Obenreizer and Vendale are discovered descending the path from the convent. They both stop when they get to the level Track. Vendale cautiously peers over the brink of the precipice.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Another precipice! A gulf frightful to see! Have we struck the Track once more?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: We have struck the Track.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: The storm seems to have passed over.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: The storm will come again.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: The convent was our last place of shelter. We left the convent half an hour since. If the storm comes back on us, where do we take refuge next?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Nowhere!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Bad news for me! I'm numbed and sleepy. I feel the drowsiness I felt last night at the inn. What does it mean?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: It means the journey is over!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Over—in this desolate pass? Over—before we have reached the top?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Over—before you have reached the top. I promised to guide you to your journey's end; and I have kept my promise. The journey of your life ends here. Nothing can prolong it. You are sleeping as you stand!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: You are a villain! What have you done to me?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: You are a fool!—I have drugged you at the convent. You are doubly a fool!—I drugged you last night at the inn! You are trebly a fool!—I am the thief and the forger. In a minute more, I shall take the proof against me from your dead body!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.stage: (confusedly; feeling the influence of the laudanum).
sp.p: Would you murder me in cold blood? You villain! what have I done to you?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Done? George Vendale! you shall hear what you have done. I love Marguerite! I sacrificed my honour, I took the money which was not mine, to buy luxuries for her! I love Marguerite—and you are the man who has come between us! You are the man who hounded me into buying the diamonds! You maddened me into spending the money which would have replaced the missing sum! You led to the discovery that the sum was missing! You carry my ruin at this moment in the pocket of your coat! You disgrace me in her eyes, if you live to see her again! You die! If you had a thousand lives, you die!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Stand off! Coward! murderer! Stand off!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Murderer? I don't touch you! I take the paper—I leave you here—and you die. I can wait! You will be asleep in two minutes; any sleep in the snow is death; you are sleeping as you stand.

div.stage: (Approaches Vendale.)

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.stage: (shaking off the stupor for the moment).
sp.p: Stop! Stand back from me! God bless my Marguerite—may she never know how I died! Stand back, and let me look at your murderous face! Let it remind me of something left to say!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Curse him! how he glares at me!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: No! no! no! Villain as you are, I must say the words. Obenreizer! the trust of the dead—Obenreizer! the money! the money!

div.stage: (He sinks on the brink of the precipice, still looking at Obenreizer.)

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.stage: (stooping over him, to unbutton his coat over the breast).
sp.p: Now—or never!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Never!

div.stage: (He thrusts Obenreizer back, with a last effort—and rolls himself over the brink of the precipice.)

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.stage: (looking over the brink with a cry of horror).
sp.p: He has flung himself into the abyss! Lost beyond all human finding! Dead in the gulf beyond human reach!
sp.stage: (He starts back from the precipice. The sky darkens, the lightning quickens; the thunder and the wind grow louder. The bells of the convent are heard faintly in the far distance.)
sp.p: Oh, Marguerite! what shall I say when you ask me for him?
sp.stage: (The thunder bursts in a louder peal.)
sp.p: The vengeance of Heaven thunders on me! Cain! Cain! Cain! Where is thy brother?

div.stage: (He rushes out on the left. At the same moment, the dogs from the convent, and a Monk, bearing a torch, appear at the top of the path, on the right. They are followed by Marguerite and Joey Ladle, and by other Monks carrying torches and ropes.)

sp.speaker: First Monk
sp.p: Footsteps here! No accident, so far. They have passed this way!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Footsteps trampled backwards and forwards! I can see it! Too late! too late! He has killed him here!

sp.speaker: First Monk
sp.stage: (pointing to the ground on the left).
sp.p: No! The footsteps go on from this place. They had left us half an hour before you reached the convent. They will gain the next refuge before the storm bursts again.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Look closer! The steps are the steps of one man only! The dogs! look at the dogs!

div.stage: (The dogs drag the men who hold them to the brink of the precipice, and bark furiously. Marguerite hurries to the edge to look over.)

sp.speaker: Joey
sp.p: Hold her back! For the love of Heaven, hold her back!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Hold him back! I'm mountain born. It's he who is in danger. The torches! the torches!
sp.stage: (Two Monks advance to the edge with torches. Others hold Joey back by main force. Marguerite looks over the abyss—and starts to her feet with a scream.)
sp.p: I see him!

sp.speaker: First Monk
sp.p: Where?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: There! on the shelf of ice that stretches over the torrent! There! there! there!
sp.stage: (She turns and appeals to the Monks.)
sp.p: The ropes! Where are the ropes?

sp.speaker: Two Monks.
sp.p: Here!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Are these the only ropes?

sp.speaker: First Monk.
sp.p: The only ropes here. There are stronger ropes and newer ropes at the refuge above. Fetch them, one of you!

div.stage: (A Monk ascends the path, and disappears at the top.)

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: His life may hang on moments! I am the lightest among you. Give me the ropes!

sp.speaker: The Monks.
sp.p: You!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Give me the ropes, and lower me down to him!

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: For the Lord's sake, don't listen to her! For the Lord's sake, don't give her the ropes!

sp.speaker: First Monk.
sp.p: The risk is too dreadful at that depth! The man is dead!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Alive or dead, I will bring him up or die with him! I am a peasant! In these frightful places I know no giddiness or fear. He is my promised husband! I passionately love him! He will die before the Monk gets back from the refuge!
sp.stage: (She snatches the ropes from the men who hold them.)

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Take them away from her! If you are men, take them away from her!

sp.speaker: First Monk.
sp.p: My poor girl, we pity you. Don't force us to take the ropes from you!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Good men! Blessed friends of travellers! look at me! I was born among the mountains—I have seen this done before! Watch my hands! If they falter or go wrong, make me your prisoner by force! If they are steady and go right, help me to save him!

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Look at her! Look at her!

sp.speaker: The Monks.
sp.p: She is inspired!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: I am inspired, by Heaven's mercy.
sp.stage: (She fastens the last knots—ties the ropes together—sets her foot on them and tries the strain herself—then holds the ends out to the Monks to try the strain with their own hands.)
sp.p: Sling the brandy and the wine round me! and lower me down to him!

sp.speaker: First Monk.
sp.p: Think again! Think again! He must be dying or dead!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Dying, or dead, my husband's head shall lie on my breast—or I will dash myself to pieces!

sp.speaker: First Monk.
sp.p: One moment more—and you shall have your way. Brother Francis may be coming back with the stronger rope.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: My husband is perishing in that frightful deep! The rope that will not support you men, will support me.
sp.stage: (She slings the flasks of brandy and wine round her.)
sp.p: I claim your promise. Lower me down!
sp.stage: (She leads the way to the precipice, and flings back the loose ends of the ropes to the Monks.)

sp.speaker: First Monk
sp.p: One brother here, with me! Two brothers at the other end. Hold the torches high! God bless and preserve her! Lower away!

div.stage: (The Monks not occupied with the ropes fall on their knees. Joey kneels with them. All fervently repeat the words, “God bless and preserve her!” Marguerite is lowered, inch by inch, with anxious care. A pause of silence when her head has disappeared behind the edge.)

sp.speaker: First Monk.
sp.p: Are you safe?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: I am safe.

sp.speaker: First Monk.
sp.p: Is he dead?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: He is insensible. His heart beats. It beats against mine.

sp.speaker: First Monk.
sp.p: How does he lie?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: On a ledge of ice. It has thawed beneath him. It will thaw beneath me. We shall die together. I am content.

sp.speaker: First Monk
sp.stage: (turning, and holding up the ropes before the rest).
sp.p: The strands are frayed on the edges of the rock. The ice is melting under her—and these ropes can be used no more. Do you see our brother?

sp.speaker: The Monks.
sp.p: No sign of him yet!

sp.speaker: First Monk.
sp.p: The new rope! the new rope!

div.stage: (Brother Francis appears at the top of the path.)

sp.speaker: First Monk
sp.p: Courage! the new rope is coming. How goes it?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: His heart still beats. I warm him in my arms. The ice melts under us.

sp.speaker: First Monk
sp.p: The rope! The rope!
sp.stage: (Brother Francis hurries down with the rope. The First Monk calls down to Marguerite once more.)
sp.p: The rope is here! How goes it?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: We are sinking faster. We are deadly cold. His heart beats no more.

sp.speaker: Joey
sp.stage: (breaking away from the Monks, and snatching the rope out of Brother Francis's hands).
sp.p: Give it to me, or I shall do some of you a mischief! Here's a rope that will bear anything. Knot it round me, some of you! and let me down to her.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Let no one down. The ice will bear no new weight. Lower the rope only.

sp.speaker: First Monk.
sp.p: Lift the torches! and keep that man back from the precipice.
sp.stage: (The rope is lowered. The First Monk continues, looking over.)
sp.p: She is fastening the rope round him!—No! No! Round yourself!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: He is dearer to me than myself. There may be time to save him yet. Raise him! Softly!

div.stage: (The insensible body of Vendale is drawn up, and laid on the ground. The First Monk and his assistants instantly lower the rope again to Marguerite. Joey breaks away for the second time—lifts Vendale's head on his knee, and lays his hand on Vendale's heart.)

sp.speaker: First Monk
sp.p: Have you got the rope round you?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Yes. Is he safe above?

sp.speaker: First Monk.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Is his heart beating?

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: His heart is still for ever!

div.stage: (The Monks at the rope, all bending together, lay the first strain on it, for the raising of Marguerite. The curtain falls.)

div.head: First Scene.
div.stage: —The office of the Notary in the Swiss village. In the flat scene, on the left of the centre, a practicable door, supposed to lead into an ante-chamber to the room represented on the stage. In the flat scene also —on the right of the centre—a practicable iron door studded with nails. The door has neither keyhole nor handle—no visible means of opening it from the outer side. On the right-hand side of the stage, a large window, on the English plan, supposed to look out on a garden. On the left-hand side of the stage, a second door, serving for entrances and exits. A table covered with papers near the window. A lamp burning on the table. A candle and matches near it. Writing materials on the table. Obenreizer and Maître Voigt discovered, seated.)

sp.speaker: Maître Voigt.
sp.p: You come late, my good friend. But, late or early, you are equally welcome! There! there! Don't be cast down. You will begin a new life to-morrow morning in my office.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: The gratitude is here. But the words to express it are not here.

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: Ta—Ta—Ta! Don't talk to me about gratitude. I hate to see a man oppressed. I see you oppressed, and I hold out my hand to you by instinct. Your father sent me my first client. Do I owe nothing to your father's son? I owe him a debt of friendly obligation, and I pay it to you.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Do me one last favour, sir—don't act on impulse. Hear the case for and against me, before you take me into your office.

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: I know it already!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Pardon me, sir, you have only a general knowledge of it. I owe it to you as well as to myself to go a step farther and to tell you the details.

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: As you will. You speak well, my son. You will be a fine lawyer one of these days.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: My troubles begin with the accidental death of my late travelling-companion—my lost dear friend, Mr. Vendale.

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: Ah! yes, yes. Vendale? It's a droll circumstance, that I should once have had a client named Vendale!—Where have I put my snuff-box?

div.stage: (Searches among the papers on the table.)

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: A client named Vendale? Vendale is a very uncommon name. I'll make a note of that!
sp.stage: (Finds Maître Voigt's snuff-box, and hands it to him.)
sp.p: As I was saying, sir, my troubles begin with the death of my dear friend, Mr. Vendale. What follows? I save myself. I go down to Milan. I am received with coldness by Defresnier and Company. I am discharged by Defresnier and Company. Why? I ask, do they assail my honour? No answer. I ask, where are the proofs that condemn me? No answer. I ask, what am I to think? The reply is, “Think what you like, and go.” That is all. I ask you, sir, is that enough?

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: That is not enough. You can rebut assertion. But how can you rebut silence?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: How indeed! But the cruelty of the case does not stop there.

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: Yes, yes, I have heard. Your ward—Mademoiselle Marguerite—rebels against you next.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: “Rebels” is too soft a word. My ward revolts from me with horror. My ward withdraws herself from my authority. I don't even know where she is! She writes that I shall never see her again. She refers me, if I want to write, to Mr. Bintrey.

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: And I write to him on your behalf. And Mr. Bintrey writes back that he is coming to confer with me here. Where is his letter?

div.stage: (Searches again among the papers on the table.)

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Let him come! Have I no legal rights?

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: Certainly! All but felons have their legal rights.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: And who calls me felon?

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: Nobody. Be calm under your wrongs.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Mr. Bintrey is coming here to dispute my authority over my ward.

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: Your authority is unassailable until your ward is of age.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: I will enforce my authority! I will make her submit to it. I owe it to you, sir, who have befriended me, to assert myself openly.

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: Quite right! Quite right! Don't excite yourself—don't think of it again till there is a necessity for thinking of it. Come to-morrow, and I will teach you your new duties in my office.
sp.stage: (Shuffling among the papers on the table.)
sp.p: Oh! these papers, these papers, there is the devil's own confusion among them from morning to night. Two bundles tied with blue ribbon—papers that are done with, and that ought to be put away. Where are they?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Here is one of them, sir. I can't find the other.

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: No matter! The clerk may have put the other bundle away.
Ah! my poor back! The rheumatism again!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Let me save you the trouble, sir. Let me put these papers away.

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: You put them away!
All my papers of importance are kept there. You want to put these away? Suppose you try!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: A chance of discovering where the Vendale papers are kept!
sp.stage: (Tries to open the door, and finds neither handle nor lock to open it by.)
sp.p: No handle, no bolt, no key, and no keyhole!
sp.stage: (Pointing towards the door on the left.)
sp.p: There is a second door to your strong-room, on that side?

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: There is no second door!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Then there is a window?

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: Nothing of the sort. The window has been bricked up. Listen at the door, and tell me if you hear nothing inside?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Clockwork!

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: Aha!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: I know! I heard of this years ago when I was a watchmaker's apprentice at Geneva. Perrin Brothers have finished their famous Clock-lock at last. And you have got it!

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: Bravo! The Clock-lock it is! I possess the greatest curiosity in Europe! No thief can steal my keys. No burglar can pick my lock. No power on earth can move that door till my little sentinel inside—my worthy friend who goes Tick-Tick as I tell him—says Open! That—
—for all the thieves in Christendom!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Pardon my curiosity, dear sir! May I see it in action?

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: By all means! Look at your watch. What time is it now?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Within a minute of half-past ten.

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: Within a minute you will see the door open by itself.
sp.stage: (A pause. A clock on the chimney-piece strikes the half-hour. The iron door silently opens back of itself. To the inner side of the door is attached a wooden case. In the middle of the case is a large white clock-dial. The figures denoting the hours are in their usual places. But the clock has only one large hand, and is without the usual glass-case. Maître Voigt lights the candle on the table, and crosses to show the lock to Obenreizer. The light thus thrown on the strong-room shows it to be filled with boxes and papers. Maître Voigt takes the papers from Obenreizer's hand, and puts them away before he explains the action of the lock.)
sp.p: There! We'll put the papers away first. Now! look at my grand curiosity!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: A common clock! No! not a common clock. It has only one hand.

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: That hand, my friend, goes all round the dial. As I put it, so it regulates the hour, or the part of an hour, at which the door shall open. The hand points to half-past ten at night. As you saw for yourself, at halfpast ten the door opened.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: You set the hand—and the door opens, when you like, in the twenty-four hours?

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: When I like. My good friend Tick-Tick follows the time like any other clock, and opens when I tell him. You shall see me give Tick-Tick his orders for tomorrow. It is late—I leave my office at once—I return no more till to-morrow at eight! Good! I put the hand to eight. I close the door again—and no power on earth, not I myself, can open it, before eight to-morrow morning.

div.stage: (Attempts to close the door. Obenreizer stops him.)

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Hadn't you better make sure, sir—?

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: Make sure of what?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: That the other bundle of papers is not on the table—before you close the door?

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: Ah! my friend, you are a better man of business than I! Quite true. Hold the candle for me. It is as well to make sure.

div.stage: (Goes back to the table and looks among the papers.)

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: The Vendale papers must be here! I'll have them to-night! I'll put the hand to eleven!

div.stage: (Changes the hand to eleven, and blows out the candle.)

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: No! the other bundle is not here. The clerk must have put it away. What! the candle out?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Some sudden draught, sir, I suppose, from the window.

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: Likely enough. My window is made on the English plan. The English are a people who adore draughts. Go, and light the candle again. I will shut the door. There!
Good night, my friend Tick-Tick! You open no more till to-morrow morning.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: It opens in half an hour!

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: Thank you! Thank you! Now we'll turn the lamp down—and then we'll say good night. At eight to-morrow. I'll light you over the stairs.
sp.stage: (Stops on the way out, and points to the door of the safe.)
sp.p: Aha! my friend, there's an invention to puzzle a thief! Other lawyers have their anxious moments. I know that my papers are safe.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Absolutely unassailable, my dear sir, as you say!

div.stage: (He goes out by the door on the left, Maître Voigt follows him, says “Good night” outside, and then returns alone to the room.)

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: My snuff-box—where is my unlucky devil of a snuff-box?
My handkerchief—where is that inveterate wanderer, my handkerchief?
My newspaper—where, in the name of Heaven, are my politics?
Ah! I have recovered my politics. My friend Tick-Tick—good night again, and pleasant dreams!

div.stage: (He goes out by the side door, and is heard to lock and double-lock it outside. The stage remains empty and dark for a moment. Then a ray of moonlight appears through the garden window. The window is lifted, and the dark figure of Obenreizer appears in the moonlight getting into the room.)

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: All quiet!
The door locked outside—Maître Voigt gone away for the night.
A few minutes more, and the Clock-lock will betray its master's secrets.

The Vendale papers! Let me think. What were those last words he said to me on the mountain? He asked to look in my face. What did that mean? Impossible to guess. He spoke of money—he spoke of the trust of the dead. If that means anything, it means that he had a crime on his conscience. Let me discover that crime—and I blacken his memory in Marguerite's estimation! I weaken the hold that he still has on her, even in his grave! I give Time, that changes everything, the chance of changing her heart towards me!
Will the door never open? Hush!
sp.stage: (The clock on the chimney-piece strikes eleven.)
sp.p: Now! Now!
sp.stage: (The door silently opens back. Obenreizer snatches out of the safe the boxes and papers. He puts them down in the ray of moonlight, and opens and examines them eagerly.)
sp.p: The names are on the boxes! Where is his name?
No!—No!—No!—Stop! Am I right? Yes! here is the name!—Vendale!
sp.stage: (The noise of an opening door heard outside below.)
sp.p: A door opening! Somebody coming this way! I haven't a moment to lose.
sp.stage: (Snatches the papers out of the Vendale box, and puts them in the pocket of his coat. Collects all the boxes and the other papers, and throws them pell-mell into the safe, closing the door. As he makes for the window, the key is heard turning in the lock of the side door on the left.)
sp.p: Just in time!

div.stage: (The moment after Obenreizer has closed the window from the outside, Maître Voigt enters with a candle in his hand, leading in Bintrey.)

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: This way, Mr. Bintrey! Who would ever have expected to meet you at the inn door at this time of night? Didn't I see somebody with you?

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Never mind that now—you see me. You got my letter, telling you I was coming? There were delays on the road, or you would have seen me here sooner.
B-r-r-r-r! it's cold in these parts!

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: Shall I light the fire?

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: No! no! Never mind. Perhaps this room is warmer!
sp.stage: (He goes to the door supposed to lead into the ante-chamber, opens it, and looks in.)
sp.p: No! not a bit warmer! A nice little room, though. An ante-chamber to this—eh? With a window looking out on a garden—and a fine bright moon in the sky which will be peeping in at the window before long!

A pretty place this, my worthy brother-lawyer, for an office! Our offices in London are as shabby and hideous as offices can be. Bare, barren, and business-like, all begin with a B in England, Maître Voigt!

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: What can I do for you, Mr. Bintrey?

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: You can first excuse my disturbing you at this time of night. And then, you can bring me within speaking distance of Mr. Obenreizer as soon as you please!

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: My dear sir, it's past eleven o'clock. Can't you wait till to-morrow?

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: I could—with anybody but Obenreizer. My way with him is to take him by surprise.

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: You distrust my friend Obenreizer? Ah! you do him an injustice there!

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Time will show which of us does justice to your friend. The first thing is to find him. I am sorry to have disturbed you. I'll go myself and inquire at the inn.

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: Quite useless! Mr. Obenreizer has some unpleasant association with the inn. He is lodging somewhere at the other end of the village.
sp.stage: (A knock is heard at the side door.)
sp.p: Who's there?

sp.speaker: A Voice outside.
sp.p: The night watchman, Maître Voigt!

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: Come in!

div.stage: (The Watchman enters, bringing in Obenreizer.)

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Here he is!

sp.speaker: The Watchman
sp.p: I found this man, Sir, hanging about under your garden-wall.

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: Nonsense! This gentleman is a friend of mine. A complete mistake—

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Nothing of the sort! Mr. Watchman, you never did a cleverer thing in your life. You have brought the very man here whom I wanted to see! Accept a small token of my esteem for an officer of the law.

sp.speaker: The Watchman.
sp.p: Heaven bless your worship! I hope the next rascal who falls into my hands may be worth as much to me!

div.stage: (Exit by the side door.)

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Mr. Bintrey, what that ignorant fool says or does is a matter of no earthly importance. What you say demands special attention. You expressed yourself just now as wanting to see me. Why, if you please, at this time of night?

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: You shall have every necessary explanation in one moment. Maître Voigt—

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: My good friend Obenreizer, take a seat.

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.stage: (takes Maître Voigt to the other side of the stage, and points to the door which he has previously opened. While he and Maître Voigt speak apart, Obenreizer takes the Vendale papers from his pocket, and furtively looks at the inscription outside them).
sp.p: Nobody likely to be in there at this time of night?

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: Nobody.

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Give me pen, ink, and paper; and place your servant at my disposal. I have a reason.
sp.stage: (Whispers in Maître Voigt's ear. Maître Voigt starts violently, and looks at Obenreizer. Bintrey continues.)
sp.p: Do what I ask—and you'll see the result.
sp.stage: (Maître Voigt gets the writing materials, and rings the bell. Bintrey scribbles two lines hastily. Obenreizer speaks to himself, still looking at the inscription on the Vendale papers.)

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: “Affairs of Mr. Vendale—Private.” While those two old fools keep me here, there is no looking at what is inside.
sp.stage: (Puts the papers back in his pocket, and addresses Bintrey.)
sp.p: Mr. Bintrey! these are not business hours. I will see you tomorrow morning.

div.stage: Enter Maître Voigt's Servant by the side door.

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: One moment, my dear sir, one moment!
Take this note to its address, and wait for further directions.
sp.stage: (The Servant goes out with the note. Maître Voigt peeps uneasily through the ante-chamber door. Bintrey addresses Obenreizer.)
sp.p: Mr. Obenreizer, we have a proverb in England which tells us that “a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.” There is no knowing what may happen before to-morrow. I have an appeal to make to your generosity, which there is an urgent necessity for making to-night.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: In the presence of Maître Voigt?

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: In the presence of my worthy brother-lawyer, and of your friend.
Sit down, my good sir, sit down. And excuse my addressing that invitation to you in your own office.

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: My English comrade is a terrible man!

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: My Swiss colleague is a mere child!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: There is some motive under all this. I'll find it out!
Mr. Bintrey, you have another proverb in England—“Take time by the forelock!” Don't let me hurry you!

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: My dear sir, I'm infinitely obliged to you for the hint! You are a man of decision—it's a perfect luxury to do business with you. There has been a misunderstanding between you and your ward. I am here to represent your ward.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: In other words, you, a lawyer, are here to represent an infraction of the law.

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: What a head that man has got! How admirably he puts his points!

Ah! my dear friend!—may I call you my dear friend?—if all the people I have to deal with were only like you, what an easy profession mine would be! Don't let us talk about the law. I declare I am afraid to encounter you in a matter of law. My business here is to make a compromise between you and your ward. Let us make it!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: There must be two parties to a compromise. I decline to become one of them. The law gives me authority to control the actions of my ward. I insist on my authority.

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: One word, Mr. Obenreizer—

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Not a syllable, my good sir! Bless my soul! does he want your assistance? No! he is formidable enough by himself.

I never met with a man that I cottoned to like you! You'll get on the blind side of me if you go on like this! Don't abuse your influence—pray don't abuse your influence. Now let me put it in another way. For the sake of peace and quietness, for the sake of your own dignity, relax your authority a little.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: You are wasting your time and mine. If my ward is not rendered up to my authority within one week from this day, I invoke the law. If you resist the law, I take her by force!

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: No! no! no! Now do hear me!

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: My good creature, will you be quiet? Hear you? Why, the man is granite! I can think of nothing comparable to Mr. Obenreizer but granite —and even that wears out in course of time!

My admirable friend! let me respectfully suggest one consideration. All justice—even your justice —gains by being tempered with mercy. Have some pity on the poor girl! Remember how lately she lost her lover by a dreadful death! Will nothing move you?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Nothing! You have heard my last word. Good night!

div.stage: (The Servant enters and gives Bintrey a note.)

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.stage: (to the Servant, after looking at the note).
sp.p: All right. Do as you are told.
sp.stage: (The Servant goes out. Bintrey continues, addressing Obenreizer.)
sp.p: One last word before you go.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: One last word to you. You may impose on your own thick-headed countrymen—but you can't impose on me. There has been something going on under the surface all through this interview. And you are at the bottom of it.

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: For the last time, won't you relent?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: For the last time, I tell you, No! And, what is more, your spy is welcome to hear it in the next room.

div.stage: (Points to the ante-chamber door.)

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: My spy!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: There is somebody listening in there!

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: There are two people listening.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Who are they?

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: You shall see!
sp.stage: (He turns towards the door, and calls loudly.)
sp.p: Come in.

div.stage: (The door is opened from within. The moon is seen streaming across the threshold. Standing in the light of the moon, Marguerite and Vendale are discovered together. Obenreizer, with a cry of horror, falls back into a chair. Maître Voigt hurries to him in alarm.)

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: Sir! sir! you have frightened him dreadfully!

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Have I? Then I've done what I wanted to do.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: The dead alive!
Stand between us, and hide him from me!

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Yes! The end is answered, sure enough!
sp.stage: (He turns to Vendale and Marguerite, who have remained together on the threshold of the ante-chamber.)
sp.p: The object of your appearance here is accomplished. There is no further fear of him now. Do you wish to be present, and to hear what I say to him next?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: The very sight of him horrifies me!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: You have made him powerless for further harm. There is no pleasure to me in seeing him humbled as well.

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Leave us, then. I'll join you in ten minutes at the inn.

div.stage: (The door closes on Vendale and Marguerite. Bintrey returns to Obenreizer.)

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: Give him time!

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: I won't! I don't know what use he may make of it if I do.
Can you listen to me?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Is he gone?

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: See for yourself!
sp.stage: (Obenreizer looks up, and draws a deep breath of relief.)
sp.p: Now take the only explanation I have to give you, in two words. You were suspected, and followed every step of the way from England. Your ward recovered the body of your victim. Your ward directed the after-efforts which restored him to life. While he lay helpless six weeks since, she wrote to me to come out to her. I received that letter in London. I also received and answered a letter from our friend here. When I reached the place where Mr. Vendale was lying ill, I found him out of danger. I was free to devote myself—and I did devote myself—to hastening the day of reckoning with you. Do you understand me, so far?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Go on.

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Defresnier and Company turned you off on suspicion, acting on information supplied by me. Having stripped you of your false character, the next thing to do was to strip you of your authority over your ward. To reach this end, I had no hesitation in digging the pitfall under your feet in the dark. Your ward's place of residence in Switzerland was kept a secret, by my advice, till Mr. Vendale was well enough to be produced as I have produced him here. There was but one certain way of shaking the devilish self-control which has hitherto made you a formidable man. That way has been tried, and it has succeeded. The last thing to do now, is to set your ward free.
You see these two papers?

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: I see them.

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: You have attempted murder, and you have committed forgery and theft. We have the evidence ready against you in both cases. Sign that paper, resigning all authority over your ward, and pledging yourself never to be seen in England or in Switzerland again. On my side, I'll sign this indemnity which secures you against further proceedings on our part. There's no other way out of it. It's a case of No Thoroughfare for you—if ever there was one yet!
After you, if you please!
sp.stage: (Obenreizer signs in silence. Bintrey signs next. They exchange the papers.)
sp.p: By daybreak tomorrow, you will cross the mountain, on your way over the frontier. I shall have you looked after by people who will see that you do it.
sp.stage: (Folding up the paper signed by Obenreizer.)
sp.p: Your fangs are drawn—you may leave us, Mr. Obenreizer, whenever you please!

div.stage: (He turns to Maître Voigt.)

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.stage: (at the side door, drawing the Vendale papers an inch or two out of his side-pocket).
sp.p: My fangs are drawn? Wait a little, till I've read these!

div.stage: (He goes out.)

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Well, Maître Voigt, what do you say to my view of your client now?

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: I am speechless with astonishment!

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: I'm devilish glad to hear it!

Don't apologise, pray! We haven't had time to be civil to each other, yet—have we? Let's be civil now. Maître Voigt! I am charmed to have had the honour of making your acquaintance. Vive la Suisse! Pray shake hands!

sp.speaker: Maitre V.
sp.p: Vive l'Angleterre!
Pray don't hurt me!

div.stage: (As the two shake hands, the Scene closes on them.)

div.head: Second Scene.
div.stage: —The approach to the village church. A bright morning. Bintrey's voice heard outside.

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Let nobody speak but me! I insist on managing everything!

div.stage: (Enter Bintrey, leading Marguerite. They are followed by Vendale, leading Sally Goldstraw, and by Joey, unwillingly led by Madame Dor. Maître Voigt brings up the rear.)

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: May I ask you one question?

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: You may do anything you like!
sp.stage: (Marguerite draws him aside from the rest. While she and Bintrey are speaking, Joey is protesting in dumb show, and Vendale and Sally are remonstrating with him.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Am I wrong—or did I hear his voice last night at the inn?

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Obenreizer's?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: You did hear him.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: What did he want?

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: He wanted to speak to you; and he wanted to speak to me. I had him dismissed—of course without seeing him—by the people at the inn. He sent me a letter next—which I sent back to him unopened. At daybreak this morning, the authorities were on the look-out for him by my directions. They saw him safe off, on his way over the mountain. You have nothing to fear —we have all seen the last of him.
Now then! what is the matter there?

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: I should wish to say a word, Mr. Bintrey, before we go any farther.

sp.speaker: Madame Dor
sp.p: I should wish to say another!

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Madame Dor endowed with speech! The age of miracles has come back!

sp.speaker: Madame Dor
sp.stage: (embracing Marguerite, with her back to the audience).
sp.p: Forgive me, my beautiful, for that I ever was a She-Cat!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: A she-cat!

sp.speaker: Madame Dor.
sp.p: His she-cat. In London. Engaged to sit watching my so charming mouse!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Why, you were our best friend, Madame Dor!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Certainly! How should I ever have told my secret to Marguerite, if you hadn't fallen asleep, ma'am, in the nick of time?

sp.speaker: Madame Dor.
sp.p: Asleep! A she-cat never sleeps. I heard it all!

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Has this good lady done?

sp.speaker: Madame Dor.
sp.p: Yes. I go back to my Bear.

div.stage: (Returns sideways to Joey.)

sp.speaker: Joey
sp.p: Is this here a marriage procession, or is it not?

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: It is.

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Then it's all wrong! Here's Jack in one place, and Gill in another? Why do you couple me with the she-cat? I'm not a-going to marry Madame Dor!

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: For shame, Mr. Joey!

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: What's Miss Goldstraw come out here for? Miss Goldstraw's come out here for to marry me. Then, why ain't I a-walking along with Miss Goldstraw?

sp.speaker: Sally.
sp.p: Wait a little, Mr. Joey—and you'll be walking along with me for the rest of your life!

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: You're not to monopolise your wife, before she is your wife! It's quite bad enough to monopolise a nice woman like that, afterwards!

sp.speaker: Sally.
