sp.p: And what's more, Mr. Joey, you're to remember this. A man had better not give a woman the chance—or it may end in her leaving him at the church door.

sp.speaker: Joey.
sp.p: Thank you, Miss! I'm quite satisfied.
Do you hear that? There's language! Fix it in your mind after me—and walk in the same all the days of your life.
“A woman had better not give a man the chance, or it may end in his leaving her at the church door.” Lord! how true!

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Come along! The church is crowded, and the parson's waiting!

div.stage: (He leads Marguerite out. At the same moment, the First Monk appears at the opposite side, passes behind the rest, and touches Vendale on the shoulder.)

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: You here!

sp.speaker: The Monk.
sp.p: I want a word with you in private.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Pardon me for one moment! Maître Voigt, will you take my place?

sp.speaker: Maître V.
sp.p: With infinite pleasure!

div.stage: (He gives Sally his arm.)

sp.speaker: Joey
sp.p: I say, Mister!
All right! all right! There'll be some mistake made before it's over. The topsy-turvy of this here procession is a-getting into my head through the pores.
Look here, ma'am! If you find me a-trying to marry you up yonder—just scream out “Wapours!” will you? That will bring me to my senses again.

div.stage: (They all go out, leaving Vendale and The Monk alone.)

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: We are alone. What do you wish to say to me?

sp.speaker: The Monk.
sp.p: You have travelled in Switzerland before. Do you know the season when the snow loosens, and the avalanches fall?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: This is the season.

sp.speaker: The Monk.
sp.p: When you rested at our convent, you had a companion with you on the mountain.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: He is crossing the mountain again to-day.

sp.speaker: The Monk.
sp.p: He has been dug out of the wreck and ruin of an avalanche, two hours since.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Dead?

sp.speaker: The Monk.
sp.p: Sorely injured. If he can be kept quiet, and if other medical help than ours can be obtained, it may yet be possible to save his life.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Is he here?

sp.speaker: The Monk.
sp.p: Our brethren are bringing him on a litter to this place. In less than an hour, I expect them here. In less than an hour, you may be leaving that church with your wife. There is a chance that your happiness and his misery may cross each other in the street. Spare the broken man the shock of seeing you. Spare your young wife the shock of seeing him.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: What must I do?

sp.speaker: The Monk.
sp.p: If you see our brethren standing together at the corner of the street, let it be a token to you that they are standing there to hide something. Pass on quickly, and direct your wife's attention the other way. His life may depend on his seeing nothing to disturb him.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: His life shall not be imperilled by me.

div.stage: (He goes out, on the way to the church. The Monk goes out on the opposite side.)

div.head: Third (and Last) Scene.
div.stage: —The village street. The church in the distance. A triumphal arch, bearing this inscription: “Honour and Love to Marguerite Vendale.” The street is crowded. The windows of the houses are full of sight-seers. A bright, joyous scene, except at one point, where The Monk and his brethren all stand close together, masking something behind them. Vendale and Marguerite descend the church-steps, followed by the persons who have appeared in the previous scene. The girls present strew flowers before them. They pass under the arch. Vendale notices the Monks, and is about to lead Marguerite in the opposite direction—when she stops him.)

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: The monks of the mountain! Why are they here?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: To see us pass, my love, like the rest. Forget the mountain—and come with me.

sp.speaker: A Voice
sp.p: Stop!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Oh! Did you hear that?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: His voice!

sp.speaker: The Voice.
sp.p: Stand back! I have something to say to them. Stand back! or may the next avalanche that falls, fall on your convent and on you!

div.stage: (The Monks draw back, and disclose the ghastly figure of Obenreizer, stretched on a litter.)

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Take my wife away.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: She must stay! Oh, Marguerite, remember the old times, and stay!

sp.speaker: The Monk
sp.p: Obey him if you can.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Who can look at him now, George, and remember the past? Let me stay.

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Let me go!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: No! you are his lawyer. Stay—and hear.
Give me the papers!
Lift me a little—and let me look them in the face.

sp.speaker: The Monk
sp.p: Gently! gently! Your life depends on your keeping your self-control.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: My life is nothing—my vengeance is all.
Tell Maître Voigt his Clock-lock has betrayed him. I have got at the secrets of one of his clients.
I have made a discovery—and it concerns you. Proofs that you can't dispute.
See this! A letter written when I was an infant, and you were an infant, too.

div.stage: (Attempts to open the letter, and sinks back on the litter with a groan of pain.)

sp.speaker: The Monk.
sp.p: In the name of humanity, stop him. If he reads that letter, he dies!

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.stage: (approaching the litter, and speaking with marked forbearance and compassion).
sp.p: You know that I am Mr. Vendale's lawyer. In your presence, and in your hearing, let me read the letter.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Yes! On one condition!

sp.speaker: The Monk
sp.p: Grant it, sir, without question.

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: I grant it.

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Read the letter—but suppress the name at the end. Leave that name to be first spoken in the hearing of George Vendale and his wife by Me. Promise!

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: I promise!

div.stage: (He opens the letter. Runs his eye over it—turns to the end—looks at the signature—and starts violently.)

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: What is it?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: See, George!
sp.stage: (Pointing to Bintrey, who is looking in speechless astonishment at Obenreizer.)
sp.p: See how they look at each other!

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: You! you are the man who—?

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: In the name of Heaven, what is it?

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: It is a letter written five-and-twenty years since—written by an Englishwoman settled in Switzerland. She is married, and childless. She addresses her sister in England—a widow. Her sister is to go to the Foundling, and adopt a child, and bring it out to Switzerland. Her sister is (for family reasons) to give her own name as the name of the person interested in the matter. That name is the same as the name we found when we went, as executors, and looked at the Foundling Register!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: My suspicion at the inn has come true! The man is found—and there he lies, broken, dying!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Wait a little!

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: The next proof!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Remember your promise!

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: A paper of instructions to Maître Voigt. The child is never to know his real origin—he is to believe himself to be really the son of the parents who have adopted him—the Swiss lawyer is to draw the necessary documents to carry out this object, in the present and in the future.
And you—you, of all men on earth, make he discovery that neither he nor I
could make for ourselves!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: The name! the name!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Not yet!
sp.stage: (To Bintrey, handing more papers to him.)
sp.p: Is the chain complete?

sp.speaker: Bin.
sp.p: Quite complete!
Our difficulty as executors is at an end. Here is the evidence to prove the identity of the missing man—the evidence which gives him the fortune left by Wilding's will!
sp.stage: (He turns, in great agitation, and motions towards Obenreizer.)
sp.p: Take him away! take him away! I daren't say what I must say next—in that dying wretch's presence!

sp.speaker: The Monk.
sp.p: Lift the litter!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Stand back, all of you!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: I have heard enough! You are the lost Walter Wilding! You are the missing man!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: George Vendale! its YOU who are the man! You! you! you!

sp.speaker: The Monk and Bin.
sp.p: Hush! Hush!

sp.speaker: Oben.
sp.p: Hush the winds, and the waves—you will as! soon hush me! I feel the new life leaping in me like fire Vendale! your marriage is no marriage at all! The people who adopted you, spared you the shame of knowing your origin. I have discovered it—and I cast it in your face! You are a bastard, brought up by public charity! Take that as your wedding present! Marguerite! Marguerite! Marguerite! I love you!!!

div.stage: (He falls back dead on the litter.)

sp.speaker: The Monk
sp.p: The evil spirit lived in this man—the evil spirit has destroyed him.

div.stage: (The Monks, all kneeling, collect together in their former position, so as to mask the litter.)

sp.speaker: George
sp.p: You once told me to think of your family, and then to think of mine!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.stage: (laying her head on her husband's breast).
sp.p: I never loved you, George, as I love you now!
